claims.claim: (Takeaway 2) 'The engine writes the prefix cache to the host memory and SSD tier right after the request is done.'
evidence: unified_radix_cache.py:465-467 'self.write_through_threshold = (1 if get_memory().hicache_write_policy == "write_through" else 2)'. With a threshold of 1, every new node is backed up the first time it is inserted without chunked=True.

batch_result_processor.py:353-359: when a request's last prefill chunk completes and the request is not finished, 'maybe_cache_unfinished_req(req, self.tree_cache)' runs (chunked defaults to False). This inserts the page-aligned prompt, and the insert emits BackupKV, which starts the D->H copy immediately (unified_radix_cache.py:1106-1110 -> _execute_and_commit_kv_backup; hybrid_cache_controller.py:309-337 write() -> start_writing(); cache_controller.py:802-826 submit_device_to_host + 'HICACHE_EVT d2h_submit').

Predicted-versus-observed d2h volume (split.py, all turns, prefill-end = floor64(prompt)-floor64(cached), finish = floor64(prompt+completion)-floor64(prompt)) matches the logged d2h_submit tokens within 0.03% in all 9 runs. Prefill-end share of all written tokens: x70 three_tier_to 0.811 (4,277,760 of 5,271,424), x70 three_tier_wc 0.725, x70 hbm_host 0.975, x10 0.981-0.982, x1 0.983 (56,973,504 of 57,967,616 for three_tier_to).

Timing on isolated turns (wt_timing.py: turns with no other turn in flight within ±1 s; the client clock is aligned to the server log by the median of prefetch_start minus send, 0.069 s): x70 three_tier_to has 35 such turns. Their d2h tokens between send and first token (+0.15 s) = 24,640, exactly the expected new prompt pages (35/35 turns exact). d2h at finish = 16,064 against 15,936 expected (33/35 exact). d2h between the first token and finish = 0. x70 three_tier_wc has 33 turns: 23,424 = 23,424 at prefill end and 0 between. x1 three_tier_to and x1 three_tier_wc (aligned on ReqTimeStats finish) have 1 turn each: 384 at prefill end, 576 at finish, 0 between.
claims.correction: Writes are eager but happen at two points, not only after the request is done. (1) All newly computed full prompt pages go D->H when the last prefill chunk completes. That is before the first token is returned, while the request is still decoding. (2) Only the tail goes D->H at request finish (cache_finished_req): the last partial prompt page plus the decode-generated pages. A trailing partial page of fewer than 64 tokens is never written. Each SSD write follows its host write within tens to hundreds of ms. By volume, 72-98% of host and SSD writes are made at the end of prefill.

claims.claim: The D->H write-through is triggered by the insert after each prefill chunk (cache_unfinished_req).
evidence: scheduler.py:3380-3381 'def stash_chunked_request(self, req): maybe_cache_unfinished_req(req, self.tree_cache, chunked=True)' (called at scheduler.py:3505-3511 for intermediate chunks)

unified_tree_core.py:913-918 _inc_hit_count_and_check: 'if node.evicted or chunked: return False' runs before hit_count is incremented. As a result, neither the walked nodes (unified_tree_core.py:1094-1095) nor the new leaf (_should_backup_after_insert, 1146-1151 / 1172-1175) emit BackupKV on a chunked insert.

The final non-chunked insert at batch_result_processor.py:359 walks the nodes the chunks created (hit_count 0->1 >= threshold 1, not backuped), so the write fires then. _build_backup_kv_action (unified_tree_core.py:2088-2104) also chains every non-backuped ancestor, parent first.
claims.correction: Intermediate chunk inserts (chunked=True) never trigger a backup. The whole prompt is written once, when the insert after the final chunk runs (cache_unfinished_req with chunked=False). For a 35K-token recompute (5 chunks of 8,192) the host write therefore starts only after the full prefill.

claims.claim: The host->SSD backup (h2s) is chained to D->H completion.
evidence: unified_radix_cache.py:1460-1475 _finish_write_through_ack: '... if self.enable_storage: for node_id in publish_node_ids: self.write_backup_storage(node_id)'. write_backup_storage has no other caller in UnifiedRadixCache (grep).

This ack runs in writing_check (unified_radix_cache.py:2836-2845) once the CUDA finish_event of the d2h copy is ready. writing_check is polled from check_hicache_events, which scheduler.py:3686 calls in every _get_new_batch_prefill_raw pass.

write_backup_storage -> cache_controller.write_storage (unified_radix_cache.py:1652-1663) -> backup_queue.put (hybrid_cache_controller.py:560-576). A single background thread performs the IO (hybrid_cache_controller.py:739-756, 'h2s_io').

Data (h2s_lag.py): h2s_submit tokens equal d2h_submit tokens exactly in all 6 SSD runs (5,271,296; 3,569,792; 53,918,976; 53,907,136; 57,967,168; 58,041,792). The log shows h2s_submit in the same millisecond as the matching d2h_done (e.g. x70 three_tier_to server.log lines 2263-2264, 05:16:36.896).

Lag from h2s_submit to h2s_io completion: x70 three_tier_to p50 0.021 s / p99 6.28 s / max 8.5 s; x70 three_tier_wc p50 0.020 s / p99 0.59 s; x10 p50 0.28 s / p99 1.14-1.17 s; x1 p50 0.34 s / p99 1.18-1.26 s. Most of that is queue wait behind the single backup thread (x1 queue-wait p50 0.22 s).
claims.correction: SSD writes are strictly chained: the D->H copy completes, the next scheduler pass polls the ack, and write_storage is queued to a single backup thread. Every host-written page is also written to SSD, 1:1. The SSD write therefore lands about 0.02 s (x70) to 0.3 s (x10/x1) after the host write, and again mostly at the end of prefill.

result.notes:
Method: read-only. Code was traced in /home/wanhr/sglang/python/sglang/srt. Logs were read with sudo. Scratch scripts are in /tmp/claude-1001/-home-wanhr-sglang/454133c8-c6f1-4d1f-8d97-1e8cda557a0d/scratchpad/assess/ (wt_timing.py and wt_timing_rts.py for isolated-turn timing, split.py for the prefill-end/finish volume split, h2s_lag.py, evict_cause.py, entry_lag.py).

Bottom line for Takeaway 2: 'writes right after the request is done' is inaccurate as stated. Under write_through with UnifiedRadixCache, the prompt KV (72-98% of all bytes) goes to host at the end of prefill: after the final chunk and before the first token. Intermediate chunks are deferred (chunked=True skips backup). Only the decode pages, plus the page straddling the prompt boundary, go at finish. SSD writes are chained 1:1 behind each host-write ack via _finish_write_through_ack -> write_backup_storage, with 0.02-0.34 s median lag. The motivating mechanism (a prefetched or queued request's host copy is displaced by write-through from other requests) should say 'other requests' prefill completions', which at x10/x1 include full 35K-token recomputes. That makes the write traffic partly self-inflicted by recomputation (x10/x1 write about 54-58M tokens against 5.3M at x70).

Caveats:
(1) The isolated-turn timing test only has a large sample at x70 (35/33 turns); x1 has 1 isolated turn per arm and x10 has none usable. The x10/x1 split therefore rests on code plus the exact volume match, not on direct timing.
(2) The evict_host cause classification is by adjacency of log lines, and it is unreliable at x70 because the async storage threads interleave.
(3) Container paths in server_args are /sgl-workspace/sglang. I assumed that tree is the same checkout as /home/wanhr/sglang. The EVAL-PATCH log formats match the code here.

Side finding relevant to Takeaway 1: prefetch_from_storage is invoked at scheduler entry (_add_request_to_queue, scheduler.py:3148-3158). At x1, scheduler entry itself lags the client send by p50 7.2 s and p90 47.7 s (entry_lag.py, from ReqTimeStats entry_time), and the first prefetch_start lags by the same amount. So there is a large pre-scheduler wait (cause not verified) that neither the scheduler's queue_duration nor the prefetch covers.

claims.claim: Takeaway 2 as stated: the host and HBM copies of a node share one lock status, so while the GPU is actively using a token its host copy cannot be evicted, which wastes some host capacity.
evidence: Server class: server.log line 38 of 20260922_051155_three_tier_to_NAT160 says 'Tree cache initialized: source=default impl=UnifiedRadixCache ... hicache_attached=True'. The evict_host HICACHE_EVT line is emitted at python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py:1141.
Host eviction chooses victims only from evictable_host_leaves (full_component.py:245 'for n in self.tree_core.evictable_host_leaves', :253 '_evict_host_leaf(x, ...)').

unified_tree_core.py:1889-1896 (_is_host_leaf): 'if node is self.root_node or not node.evicted: return False' / 'if not node.backuped' / 'if any(cd.host_lock_ref > 0 ...)' / 'if len(node.children) > 0: return False'. The device lock_ref is never checked. The only requirement tied to the device is that its Full copy is gone (evicted = 'component_data[FULL].value is None', unified_tree_core.py:151-156).

The locks are separate per tier, not merged: ComponentData has 'lock_ref: int = 0' and 'host_lock_ref: int = 0' (unified_cache/components/tree_component.py:50,53). acquire_component_lock(lock_host=True) increments only host_lock_ref on the anchor node (full_component.py:270-277).

Measured: after the host pool filled, the host mirror of device-resident KV averaged (time-weighted) 636,347-656,346 tokens, or 39.1-40.3% of the 1,627,648-token host pool, across all 9 HiCache runs (script scratchpad/assess/mirror.py).
claims.correction: The effect is real and large, but locking does not cause it. UnifiedRadixCache allows a host copy to be evicted only once that node's device copy has already been evicted (node.evicted). It must also be a leaf with host_lock_ref == 0. So under write_through, every device-resident node pins its host copy, whether or not a request holds it. The host tier is inclusive of the device tree (L2 contains L1). The 'waste' is the whole device pool mirrored in host memory, about 40% of L2, not just the part that running requests are using.

claims.claim: Only host copies of nodes locked by running requests (lock_ref > 0) are protected from host eviction.
evidence: _is_host_leaf (unified_tree_core.py:1889) rejects every node with 'not node.evicted', whether or not it is locked. Request locks cover only the device-resident segment of the path ('Skip the bottom evicted segment' ... 'Lock the device-on segment up to root', full_component.py:282-301). So the locked nodes are a subset of the device-resident nodes.

Mirror of idle, unlocked device KV, lower bound = M - U, where M = reconstructed device-resident backed-up tokens and U = '#token' in the batch log = max_total - (available + evictable) (pool_stats_observer.py:223), i.e. locked KV plus unfinished request tails. Time-weighted after host saturation: x70 three_tier_to 466,658 (28.7% of H, at least 71% of the mirror); x70 three_tier_wc 498,538 (30.6% of H); x70 hbm_host 219,755 (13.5%); x10 96,062-108,776 (5.9-6.7%); x1 48,181-48,331 (3.0%).

Reconstruction check (mirror.py: O = sum d2h_submit + sum prefetch 'loaded' - sum evict_host; M = sum d2h_submit + sum h2d_submit - sum evict_device): O peaks at exactly 1,627,648 = H in every run. M stays between 7,808 (the shared system prompt) and 668,096 (<= D) with no drift over 77-144 min.

The first evict_host line lands at +9.1-9.2 min (x70) and +6.2-6.3 min (x10/x1). At that point O_before = 1,627,072-1,627,648 (100% of H) and M = 647,424-660,864 (39.8-40.6% of H). This matches the client-side live set first reaching H at 9.2 / 6.4 min (liveset.py).
claims.correction: Three kinds of host copy are pinned. (a) Every node whose Full KV is still on the device, locked or idle; these are pinned until the device demotes them. (b) Host-only interior nodes that still have children; eviction goes leaf by leaf, so they free up once their subtree is gone. (c) Anchors with host_lock_ref > 0 during an in-flight transfer: the load-back anchor (unified_radix_cache.py:1487), the L3 prefetch anchor (:1778-1782) and the H2S backup (:1660-1661). Kind (c) is short-lived and needed for correctness. Kind (a) is the capacity cost. At x70 most of it is idle cached KV, not KV that running requests are using.

claims.claim: Under --hicache-write-policy write_through the host tier is inclusive of the device tree (L2 contains L1), and host copies of device-resident nodes are never reclaimed.
evidence: unified_radix_cache.py:465-467: 'self.write_through_threshold = (1 if get_memory().hicache_write_policy == "write_through" else 2)'.

unified_tree_core.py:913-933 (_inc_hit_count_and_check): returns '... not node.backuped and node.hit_count >= self.write_through_threshold'. It is called for every new leaf (:1150) and every matched node on the insert walk (:1094).

_build_backup_kv_action (unified_tree_core.py:2091-2104) also backs up every ancestor that is not yet backed up: 'while ... not (ancestor.backuped or ancestor.external_cache_stored): chain.append(ancestor)'.

The write happens at prefill end, not only when the request finishes. batch_result_processor.py:359 calls maybe_cache_unfinished_req(req, ...) with chunked=False after the last prefill chunk. Log evidence: the first 'd2h_submit nodes=1 tokens=7808' is at 05:16:12.673, while c9-t0 (t_send 0.003 s, latency 7.36 s) finishes around 05:16:18.9.
Load-back keeps the host copy: full_component.py:410-419 sets cd.value from device_indices and leaves host_value unchanged.

Invariant: device-resident nodes form an ancestor-closed subtree (full_component.py:294 'FULL invariant broken: evicted ancestor ... above device-on segment'; :367 'FULL device evict only from leaves'). So host-only nodes form the bottom fringe of the tree.

Duplicate reclaim runs only under write_back: unified_tree_core.py:1497 'if self.is_write_back and component_type == BASE_COMPONENT_TYPE: self._reclaim_full_host_duplicates(...)'. The legacy HiRadixCache (not used in these runs) has the same inclusive rule: hiradix_cache.py:1191 'if not node.evicted or node.lock_ref > 0' and :1368 'if not x.evicted: continue'.
claims.correction: Correct as stated. The host pool keeps a copy of about 95-98% of the device pool (time-weighted M/D = 0.952-0.982 after saturation), so the L1+L2 hierarchy holds about max(L1, L2) = H unique tokens, not L1+L2.

claims.claim: write_back and write_through_selective behave differently from write_through with respect to this mirror.
evidence: write_back: no backup at insert time (unified_tree_core.py:919-920 'if self.is_write_back: return False'). At device eviction an unbacked D-leaf gets a BackupKV (unified_tree_core.py:1379-1383). The demote runs only after a blocking wait: unified_radix_cache.py:750-758 calls _execute_and_commit_kv_backup(write_back=True) then writing_check(write_back=True), which at :2813-2816 does '# Blocking: wait for all pending write-backs' ... 'ack.finish_event.synchronize()'. Under host pressure, _reclaim_full_host_duplicates frees host copies of device-resident nodes, first sparing evictable D-leaves (unified_tree_core.py:1522-1552), so the hierarchy is non-inclusive. If a backup fails, the unbacked subtree is dropped (drop_subtree_no_host, :1403).

write_through_selective: threshold 2. hit_count is also incremented on matched nodes during insert (unified_tree_core.py:1094). In this agent workload the prompt leaf inserted at prefill end is walked again by the same request's cache_finished_req, so it reaches hit 2 within one turn. The mirror is therefore almost the same size. The difference is that output tails are unbacked until the next turn, and on device eviction an unbacked node is deleted instead of demoted (unified_tree_core.py:1384-1393 '# Write-through: node has no backup, delete entirely').
claims.correction: write_back is the non-inclusive design already in the codebase. It pays for that with a synchronous D2H on the eviction path. write_through_selective does not meaningfully shrink the mirror for this workload, and it turns some demotions into permanent loss.

claims.claim: Waste quantification: the share of the L2 host pool that mirrors device-resident KV, L1 = 668,160 tokens vs L2 = 1,627,648 tokens.
evidence: Measured, time-weighted mean of M after the first host eviction (mirror.py). x70: hbm_host 645,209 (39.6%), three_tier_to 655,747 (40.3%), three_tier_wc 656,346 (40.3%). x10: 639,710 / 638,883 / 639,416 (39.3%). x1: 636,388 / 636,348 / 636,347 (39.1%). p10 >= 626,176 in every run.

The host space left for content not on the device, H - M, is 971,901-991,300 tokens (59.7-60.9% of H). An exclusive hierarchy would hold H + D = 2,295,808 unique tokens, about 38-40% more than the inclusive H + (D - M) = 1.64-1.66M.

Live set of session-private KV vs capacity (liveset.py, client.jsonl, page-floored). x70 three_tier_to: at or above H for 30 of 89 min (34%), first at 9.2 min; at or above H+D for 8 min (9%), first at 20.3 min. x10 three_tier_to: 115 min (77%) vs 62 min (42%). x1 three_tier_to: 122 min (85%) vs 69 min (48%). Peak live set 2.37-2.48M tokens.
claims.correction: About 40% of the host pool, around 640-656K tokens, holds copies of KV that is already on the GPU. By the live-set measure, an exclusive L1+L2 would have pushed the start of host evictions at x70 from about 9 to about 20 min, and cut the time the live set exceeds combined capacity from 34% to 9% of the run. At x10/x1 the live set still exceeds H+D for 42-48% of the run, so removing the mirror would reduce host evictions there but not eliminate them.

claims.claim: The inclusive design buys cheap device eviction: no D2H copy on the critical path.
evidence: A write_through device eviction of a backed-up leaf is a demote. It only frees device indices (unified_tree_core.py:1394-1400 -> _demote :1629-1655, 'assert not node.evicted and node.backuped'). The D2H copy already ran asynchronously at insert time.

Measured demote cost, from the ms= field of the evict_device lines: x70 three_tier_to 52,381,056 tokens in 5,151 calls = 3,039 ms (0.59 ms/call, 0.058 us/token). x10 three_tier_to 70,691,648 tokens in 9,633 calls = 3,657 ms (0.38 ms/call, 0.052 us/token).
Measured D2H cost, from the d2h_done ms= field: 2.63-2.66 us/token (36.9-37.4 GB/s at 98,304 B/token).

Counterfactual for an exclusive or write_back-style design (every eviction copied synchronously): x10 70.69M x 2.63 us = about 186 s (about 19 ms per eviction call), vs 3.7 s measured. x70 52.38M x 2.66 us = about 139 s (about 27 ms per call), vs 3.0 s.

Load-back keeps host copies, so re-demoting loaded-back KV is also free. x70 three_tier_to loaded back 47,777,664 tokens (h2d_submit), all of which an exclusive design would have to copy again on re-eviction. Write-through also starts the L3 write immediately (unified_radix_cache.py:1471-1475, write_backup_storage on the write-through ack).
claims.correction: Correct. Inclusion makes device eviction about 50x cheaper per token and keeps D2H off the scheduler's allocation path. It also puts the host copy in place before L3 persistence starts. The cost is about 40% of L2 capacity. A design that avoids the waste needs pressure-aware reclaim of mirrors of idle device-resident nodes (the write_back _reclaim_full_host_duplicates logic exists but is gated on is_write_back at unified_tree_core.py:1497). It also needs a non-blocking re-backup, or an acceptance of drops, when those nodes are later demoted.

result.notes:
Short answer: the 'waste' in Takeaway 2 is real, but the mechanism and the regime differ from how the takeaway states them.

1. **Mechanism.** Under write_through every tree node is copied to the host. A host copy can only be evicted once its device copy is gone (unified_tree_core.py:1889). So the host copy of every GPU-resident node is pinned, whether or not a request has it locked. As a result, host eviction began exactly when the cumulative write-through volume reached L2 (1,627,584 of 1,627,648). The effective unique capacity of the two tiers is L2, not L1+L2.

2. **Size.** In x70 three_tier_to, about 40% of the host pool (≈651K tokens, ≈64 GB) duplicates L1; the hard floor is 30%. In the saturated hbm_host run it is only about 15-18%, because the GPU then holds mostly in-flight recompute KV that has no host copy yet. So the waste peaks when requests are sparse, which is Takeaway 1's regime rather than Takeaway 2's 'dense requests' framing.

3. **Novelty caveat.** The code already reclaims host copies of GPU-resident nodes, but only under write_back (unified_tree_core.py:1497-1503 `_reclaim_full_host_duplicates`, which spares evictable device leaves on its first pass). Any 'exclusive hierarchy' claim needs a write_back comparison arm (not run; I haven't checked whether write_back works with nixl L3), or should be framed as keeping write-through plus the L3 copy while reclaiming host duplicates.

**Method and caveats:**
- The free space in the device pool is never logged. I bounded it by the device-eviction overshoot; evictions happen only on demand and every ~0.3-0.5 s.
- The running-request model is validated for three_tier_to (within 1.6% of logged num_used) but not for hbm_host (it overestimates by 27% because its queue times are estimates). The hbm_host upper bound is therefore soft; its lower bound comes directly from the logs.
- The prior ~1.56M live-set figure did not reproduce exactly. My definition gives 1.615-1.618M; either way it is ≈L2.
- The LRU miss projection works at session granularity and is calibrated to an effective capacity of 0.85 x L2. Treat it as indicative.
- Only campaign 7 three_tier_to and hbm_host were analysed; three_tier_wc was not checked.

result.notes:
Code path: the server used UnifiedRadixCache with the Python tree core (SGLANG_UNIFIED_RADIX_TREE_CORE_BACKEND defaults to 'python').

Lifecycle of a returning turn:
1. On arrival, _add_request_to_queue -> _prefetch_kvcache -> init_next_round_input matches L1+L2. This match takes no lock, but it refreshes last_access_time on the matched path.
2. prefetch_from_storage is called only for the unmatched suffix. If the suffix is < 256 tokens it returns before any lock. Otherwise it host-locks the anchor, and an async L3 query runs.
3. If the query hits < 256 tokens (almost always in the dense regime, because the suffix is the brand-new tool output), revoke_pending_prefetch drops the lock within milliseconds.
4. If the query hits >= 256 tokens, pages are allocated (this can itself evict), read, inserted by insert_host at IO completion in _drain_ack_prefetch, and unlocked right away.
5. The request then waits with nothing protecting it. Host eviction is LRU by last_access_time; under FCFS that removes the longest-waiting history (the next one to be admitted) first.
6. At admission, check_prefetch_progress, then init_next_round_input re-matches L1/L2 only, then init_load_back, then inc_lock_ref. Nothing queries L3 again. The paced retry (_retry_missed_storage_prefetches) is disabled by retry_poll_interval=0.

Verdict:
- Takeaway 1 is legitimate for the sparse regime. The L3 read is fully exposed: about 19-20% of x70 returns pay 2-3 s at p50. Gaps before those turns are about 50 s or more, so there is enough lead time.
- Takeaway 2's symptom is real and very large: about 95% of prefill in x10/x1 is recompute of context that was in L1/L2 at arrival and on SSD the whole time. But its mechanism is mis-described. The prefetched-then-evicted case is only 0.4-1.9% of lost tokens. The dominant loss is that the arrival-time L1/L2 hit, which is not a prefetch, is evicted while queued and never re-fetched from L3.
- The two takeaways are one design, just-in-time tier resolution. Bind the L3->L2 fetch (and its protection) to the predicted admission time. In the sparse regime that time is about the tool return, since the queue is near zero; in the dense regime it comes from queue position.
- Required mechanism changes: re-resolve against L3 near admission; hold fetched pages locked until admission; evict queued histories in reverse admission order. Pinning all queued prefixes cannot work, because they add up to about the whole L2.
- The 'host/HBM lock' point is really inclusion: a node with a device copy is never an H-leaf, and write_through has no duplicate reclaim. That is a separate capacity idea.

Caveats:
- A (arrival match) = prompt_tokens - 1 - prefetch_start.tokens. It is L1+L2 combined; the logs do not separate the tiers.
- The hbm_host arms have no prefetch_start, so their arrival match cannot be measured. Their shared-prompt-only admission rate matches the SSD arms.
- The x10 SSD arms have no ReqTimeStats, so their waits use a TTFT proxy.
- The SSD-bandwidth feasibility figure (about 32%) is an estimate that ignores the concurrent write stream.
- The x70 TTFT gain is a first-order bound that ignores extra L2 pressure from early staging.
- Prior-art names (CachedAttention/AttentionStore, KVFlow, Continuum) are from memory and were not checked.

result.notes:
Method. I parsed the raw server.log and client.jsonl of the 4 runs (read-only via sudo). Scripts and the per-turn table are in /tmp/claude-1001/-home-wanhr-sglang/454133c8-c6f1-4d1f-8d97-1e8cda557a0d/scratchpad/assess/: t2_parse.py builds t2.pkl; t2_turns.py builds t2_turns.csv (one row per returning turn with P, C, tier split, T, M, s2h_query/io, loaded, host_hit, queue, entry, admission); t2_analyze.py, t2_queue.py, t2_l3.py, t2_occ.py, t2_backup.py, t2_lag.py and t2_extra.py compute the numbers. Other agents' files (t1*) share that directory; I did not touch them.

Definitions:
- Arrival = the prefetch_start timestamp, which equals ReqTimeStats entry_time within 1 ms.
- M = P-1-T. T is the logged new_input_tokens, sliced to max_prefix_len = P-1.
- Lost = M - C > 64 while the context was present at arrival.
- Campaign 8 (x10) SSD arms have no ReqTimeStats. Their admission time is load_back_init when present, otherwise t_send plus the estimated queue from turn_components. So the x10 wait bins are approximate; only the x1 bins are exact.

What I could not establish from the logs:
- Which specific nodes were evicted. evict_host has no rid; I used the aggregate host tokens evicted during each turn's wait window instead.
- Whether each lost context was individually still on the SSD. I infer it from h2s_done = d2h_done and zero cleanup events.
- Whether the context sat in L1 or in L2 at arrival (prefetch_start gives only the combined match). Among turns that kept their context, about 69% were admitted with a host hit and about 30% device-only.
- The real size of the pinned L1 duplicates in L2.

Main implication for the research idea: Takeaway 2 is legitimate and strongly supported under dense load, but its cause needs rewording. The main loss is not a prefetch that fires too early. It is that L2 content found at arrival is left unprotected, and LRU combined with the arrival-time refresh evicts the head of the FCFS queue first. Meanwhile the data stays on the SSD, and the engine never looks for it again after arrival.

For a system design:
- Pair just-in-time L3 fetch timed to the predicted admission with queue-aware (Belady-style) eviction, or at least protect the queue head.
- Re-check L3 near admission.
- Insert prefetched data lazily, at consumption time.
The required SSD bandwidth (about 0.69 GiB/s at x1) is feasible, and the prize is large: about 95% of prefill work is redundant recomputation.

The 100-connection client cap is a separate artifact. It adds a mean 20 s before the request reaches the server at x1 and should be fixed or excluded before the timing model for either takeaway is built.

claims.claim: T1 premise: the L3 prefetch starts when the request enters the scheduler queue, and the request cannot be admitted until the prefetch completes (wait_complete) or times out (timeout).
evidence: python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py:3148-3154 `def _add_request_to_queue(...)` ... `self._prefetch_kvcache(req)` (the prefetch is issued when the request is queued; there is no earlier trigger)

python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py:3817-3821 `prefetch_done = self.tree_cache.check_prefetch_progress(req.rid)` / `if not prefetch_done: # skip staging requests that are ongoing prefetch continue`
python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py:1871-1876 timeout = `prefetch_timeout_base + len(operation.hash_value) * self.prefetch_timeout_per_page`; :1882-1883 wait_complete returns False

Clock check (t1_a.py): prefetch_start minus client send is 16 ms at minimum and 69 ms at the median over 4,658 turns (three_tier_to), so server and client clocks line up. send(t) - (send(t-1)+latency(t-1)) - gap_slept has a median of 1 ms, so gap_slept is measured from the end of the previous reply.
claims.correction: Correct as stated. One detail matters for the design: a request whose prefetch is still running is skipped, not waited on, so later requests are admitted ahead of it.

claims.claim: T1: 'When the queue is shallow, queuing delay (near 0) can't hide the prefetch time, yielding extra delay.'
evidence: Storage-hit turns (cached_details.storage>0): 896 of 4,548 returns (19.7%) in three_tier_to and 837 of 4,509 (18.6%) in three_tier_wc (t1_b.py)

Queue depth 0 at arrival: 330 hits in _to (37%) and 325 in _wc (39%). Their TTFT means 1.07 s and 1.02 s are 0.77 s and 0.71 s above host hits in the same 4K prompt bin. Their mean fetch window is 0.74 s / 0.69 s with 0.56 s of own IO. Together they carry only 7.0% / 5.1% of all fetch-window time (t1_d.py, t1_q.py)
Queue depth 5 or more at arrival: 298 hits in _to and 307 in _wc carry 71.6% / 80.7% of fetch-window time. Mean fetch windows are 6.3-14.6 s, while own IO is only about 1.0-1.2 s (t1_q.py)

The queue depth at arrival tracks the number of pending L3 reads almost exactly: corr = 0.85 (_to) and 0.99 (_wc); mean queue depth 4.26 vs 3.16 pending reads (_to) and 4.51 vs 4.77 (_wc) (t1_q.py). In other words, the queue mostly consists of other requests waiting for L3 reads

Only one IO thread serves L3 reads: cache_controller.py:447-448 `self.prefetch_io_aux_thread = threading.Thread(target=self.prefetch_io_aux_func...)`, and :1136-1141 takes one operation at a time and runs `_page_transfer`. Consecutive s2h_io intervals overlap 4 times out of 960 reads in _to and 0 of 837 in _wc (t1_c.py)

Mean storage-hit TTFT breaks down as: send->query 0.17 / 0.09 s, waiting for the read thread 3.01 / 4.43 s, own IO 0.90 / 0.82 s, IO end->admission 0.58 / 0.03 s, admission->first token 0.52 / 0.20 s. Totals are 5.18 s (_to) and 5.57 s (_wc) (t1_d.py). During the read-thread wait, other reads kept the thread busy 99.5% (_to) and 99.7% (_wc) of the time (t1_c.py). Re-simulating a single FIFO reader released at s2h_query reproduces the observed io_end (median error -0.029 s; mean window 3.86 s simulated vs 3.91 s actual) (t1_sim.py)
claims.correction: The literal case exists: 37-39% of storage hits arrive to an empty queue and pay about 0.7 s of exposed own IO. That case is only 5-7% of the exposed fetch time, though. Most of the fetch cost (58% of storage-hit TTFT in _to, 80% in _wc) is requests waiting in line behind other storage restores, because L3 reads go through a single thread and arrive in bursts. The queue does not hide the fetch; the queue is largely made of fetches. The better motivation is that reactive, serialized L3 reads form a backlog in bursts, while the SSD sits mostly idle during the gaps.

claims.claim: (1) The part of storage-hit TTFT attributable to the L3 fetch, compared with host hits of similar prompt length, is large.
evidence: Storage-hit TTFT: mean 5.18 s / p50 2.76 s / p90 14.48 s in _to; mean 5.57 s / p50 3.34 s / p90 15.06 s in _wc. Host-hit TTFT: mean 1.09 s / p50 0.25 s in _to; mean 0.31 s / p50 0.24 s in _wc (t1_b.py)

Compared with host hits in the same 4K prompt bin, storage hits take 3.52 s longer on average in _to (68% of their TTFT) and 5.26 s longer in _wc (95%). Median excess over the bin's host median is 2.46 s / 3.08 s. Example bin 28-32K: storage median 3.11 s vs host 0.33 s in _to, 4.59 s vs 0.26 s in _wc (t1_d.py)
Also matching on queue depth (0 / 1-4 / 5-9 / 10+) gives an excess of 1.90 s (37%) in _to and 4.25 s (93%) in _wc. _to host hits are themselves slow at depth 10+, which shrinks its matched excess

Measured per turn, min(queue wait, send->io_end) is 78.5% of storage-hit TTFT in _to and 95.8% in _wc; the fetch window (prefetch_start->s2h_io) has p50 2.18 s / mean 3.91 s in _to and 2.97 s / 5.25 s in _wc; own IO p50 is 0.85 s / 0.80 s (t1_b.py)
Removing every storage-hit fetch window would cut mean TTFT over returns from 1.94 to 1.17 s in _to (-40%) and from 1.48 to 0.50 s in _wc (-66%) (t1_misc.py)
claims.correction: The fetch accounts for about 3.5-5.3 s per storage hit (68-95% of its TTFT), or 37-93% when load is matched. That is 40-66% of mean return TTFT at x70. Of this, 0.8-0.9 s is the read itself and the rest is waiting for the single read thread.

claims.claim: (2) With oracle knowledge of the next arrival, starting the fetch at (arrival - fetch_time) hides the fetch.
evidence: If each fetch window kept its observed length when moved earlier, the oracle hides 100% of it, because every gap (minimum 46.9 s in _to, 47.9 s in _wc) is longer than every fetch window (maximum 20-22 s). Resulting storage-hit TTFT: mean 1.11 s / p50 0.27 s / p90 3.38 s in _to; 0.23 s / 0.19 s / 0.36 s in _wc (t1_e.py)

A contention-aware re-simulation (single reader, measured IO durations, EDF on the true arrival) gives much less for a lead equal to the size-based read time (tokens x 98,304 B / 1.88 GiB/s): 24.0% hidden in _to, TTFT mean 4.24 s; 16.4% in _wc, TTFT mean 4.71 s. Adding 2 s to the lead gives 49.8% / 37.2% (t1_sim.py)

Fixed lead L before the true arrival (t1_lead.py): L=1 s hides 22.6% / 16.2%; L=5 s 66.6% / 54.0%; L=10 s 90.8% / 81.0% (TTFT mean 1.63 / 1.32 s, p50 0.37 / 0.32 s); L=20 s 100% / 99.9% (TTFT mean 1.27 s p50 0.37 s p90 3.83 s in _to; 0.32 s / 0.28 s / 0.48 s in _wc). In the peak phase (+1200-1500 s, 252 / 296 hits), L=10 s hides only 86.1% / 72.8%
When fully hidden, the residual storage-hit TTFT is send->prefetch_start + post-fetch wait + admission->first token: 1.27 s mean in _to (0.58 s of it post-fetch queue wait) and 0.32 s in _wc
claims.correction: Knowing the arrival time is not enough. Moving each fetch back by its own read time (about 1 s) hides only 16-24%, because concurrent restores still collide on the single read thread. Hiding 81-100% needs a lead about as long as the read backlog (10-20 s), plus reads scheduled earliest-deadline-first against the predicted arrivals. The 'fetch time' in the proposal therefore has to include the predicted L3 queueing delay, not just size/bandwidth. When fully hidden, storage-hit TTFT would fall from 5.18 to 1.27 s (_to) and from 5.57 to 0.32 s (_wc).

claims.claim: (3) The benefit holds up when the gap prediction is off: start = end_of_reply + max(0, g_hat - fetch - margin), g_hat = gap*(1+e).
evidence: Contention-aware simulation (t1_sim.py, t1_net.py); a start at or after the arrival falls back to the reactive fetch
e=+25% and e=+50% (any margin 0/2/10 s): hidden 1.3% in _to and 0.6% in _wc; TTFT unchanged at 5.12 / 5.54 s. Because gaps are 47 s or more, a 25% over-estimate pushes the start past the arrival
e=-25%, margin 2 s: 99.5% / 99.3% hidden, but 15.6% / 14.1% of prefetched contexts are expected to be evicted again before arrival. Net hidden is 84.7% / 87.8%; expected TTFT 1.86 s / 0.96 s
e=-50%, margin 2 s: 100% hidden, 41.4% / 37.2% re-evicted, net 55.0% / 63.1%; expected TTFT 3.03 s / 2.26 s. A 10 s margin makes it worse (e=-25%: net 73.7% / 79.8%)

Realistic predictors from session history (t1_pred.py): previous gap or running median of the session's gaps is within ±25% for only 34-50% of storage-hit turns. The running median under-predicts 99% of storage-hit gaps (median error -32% in _to, -43% in _wc), because the turns that miss L2 are the ones with longer-than-usual gaps. The policy end_of_reply + max(0, g_hat - 10 s) with these predictors hides 89-99% but re-evicts 32-42%: net 54-71%, plus 500-700 GiB of extra L3 re-reads (actual total reads 1,810 / 1,571 GiB)
claims.correction: The cost of a wrong prediction is lopsided. Any over-estimate of about 25% or more wipes out the whole benefit. Under-estimates hide the fetch but make the prefetched context wait in L2, where it is likely to be evicted before use. The prefetcher should aim slightly early (a small negative bias, about 10-20 s before the predicted arrival) and fall back to the reactive fetch. History-based gap predictors are not good enough here (net 54-71%). Whether tool-call-based prediction does better cannot be tested from these logs.

claims.claim: (4) Starting too early carries eviction risk: prefetched content can be evicted from L2 again before the request arrives.
evidence: Code: once the L3 read completes, the fetched pages go into the host tree with no lock on them. unified_radix_cache.py:2562-2565 calls `_handle_prefetch_result(operation)` when the IO ack arrives; :1983 `insert_host(...)`; :2024 `self.dec_host_lock_ref(last_host_node_id, anchor_lock_params)`. Parked content can therefore be evicted like any other host entry

L2 turnover (time for evict_host volume to reach the 1,627,648-token pool) at storage-hit arrivals: p10 76 / 69 s, p50 96 / 97 s, p90 167 / 209 s. Host eviction runs at 12.9-21.0K tokens/s during +900-2100 s and is near zero after +2400 s (t1_evict.py)

Empirical survival curve from the actual runs, by host tokens evicted during a return's gap as a fraction of the pool: below 0.1: 0% of 687 / 548 returns missed L2; 0.2-0.3: 15% / 13%; 0.3-0.4: 56% / 48%; 0.4-0.8: 66-89%; 0.8 or more: 100%. Returns whose content was later served from storage had a p50 of 0.61 / 0.65 pools evicted during the gap (t1_evict.py)

Prefetching as early as possible (at end of reply) would need residency p50 50 / 63 s and p90 296 / 299 s. 77% of those contexts would be evicted again (net hidden 19.0% / 13.3%), and the parked contexts would hold a time-average of 600K / 596K tokens (37% of the pool) with a peak of 100-106% of the pool (t1_evict.py, t1_net.py)

Fixed lead: L=10 s re-evicts 1.2% / 0.8% (net 90.0% / 80.6%, 5% of the pool parked on average during +900-2100 s); L=20 s re-evicts 7.3% / 4.9% (net 93.0% / 95.9%, 12-14% of the pool parked, peak 27%); L=30 s re-evicts 25% / 20% (net 71% / 78%); L=60 s re-evicts 64% / 56% (net 26% / 28%) (t1_lead.py, t1_park.py)
claims.correction: The eviction risk is real. The SSD is most congested exactly when L2 turnover is fastest (+900-2100 s, host eviction at 13-21K tokens/s), because both come from the live working set exceeding L2. So the usable lead is narrow. The lower bound is the read backlog (about 10 s). The upper bound is the L2 survival knee (about 0.3 of the pool evicted, roughly 20-30 s at peak rates). As-early-as-possible prefetching defeats itself (77% re-evicted). An early prefetch should either pin its pages until arrival or be counted against the L2 budget.

claims.claim: SSD read bandwidth contention: L3 restores bunch up in time, and spreading them over the gaps would lower peak demand relative to the 1.88 GiB/s ceiling.
evidence: Reads total 960 ops / 1,810 GiB in _to (64 of them timed out) and 837 ops / 1,571 GiB in _wc, spread over about 3,000 s of reads. Average demand is 0.60 / 0.53 GiB/s, and the read thread is busy 27.0% / 23.0% of that span (t1_c.py, t1_bw.py)
Per-read throughput: p50 1.93 GiB/s (about the 1.88 GiB/s ceiling), p90 4.2 GiB/s (probably page-cache hits) (t1_b.py)

Five-minute bins (t1_ts.py): 811 of 896 _to hits and 807 of 837 _wc hits fall in +900-2100 s. In +1200-1500 s the read thread is busy 85.5% / 88.8% (1.59 / 1.77 GiB/s) and the mean fetch window is 6.5 / 10.2 s. After +2100 s it is 13% busy or less, with fetch windows under 1 s
Up to 19 / 23 fetch windows are in flight at once, and 3 or more are in flight 16.4% / 14.7% of the time (t1_bw.py)

Reactive offered read demand (bytes released at s2h_query, per window): 10 s windows peak at 4.09 / 3.94 GiB/s (about 2.1x the ceiling) and exceed the ceiling 10.6% / 9.3% of the time; 60 s windows peak at 2.33 / 2.51 GiB/s (6.7% / 6.5% above the ceiling); 300 s windows peak at 1.77 / 1.86 GiB/s (94-99% of the ceiling). Achieved read throughput peaks at 1.96-2.10 GiB/s over 10-30 s, so the SSD was saturated during bursts

Spreading each restore uniformly over its whole gap cuts the 60 s peak to 1.90 / 2.22 GiB/s and time above the ceiling to 0.63% / 6.2%. Spreading over only the last 25% of the gap: 2.10 / 2.37 GiB/s, 2.35% / 6.5% (t1_bw.py)
SSD writes (write-through h2s) during the same span add 326 / 171 GiB, peaking at 1.12 / 0.21 GiB/s over 10 s windows

In _to, 64 reads (98 GiB) were cut off by the timeout after waiting a mean 7.42 s for the read thread. Those turns ran with about 8K cached tokens out of 25K and had a mean TTFT of 10.41 s (t1_misc.py)
claims.correction: Bursts are the main problem: short-window demand reaches about 2x the SSD ceiling. Over 5 minutes of the peak phase, though, demand is 94-99% of the ceiling, so shifting reads in time only smooths the bursts; it cannot add bandwidth. The EDF simulation shows a 10-20 s lead is enough to absorb the bursts at this utilization. At higher gap density (more L2 misses per second), no amount of lead would help. Write-through traffic competes for the same SSD and should be scheduled alongside the reads.

claims.claim: T1 premises: the private context is bound to be reused in the next round, and the agent's gap is predictable.
evidence: Of end-of-reply events, 4,548 of 4,676 (97.3%) in _to are followed by another turn of the same session; 128 are final turns (t1_q.py). Storage hits restore a mean of 20.3K (_to) / 20.5K (_wc) tokens of the previous context, out of prompts of about 29K

Gaps are the trace pre_gap x70, capped at 1,200 s: return gaps p10 3.7 s, p50 49.1 s, p90 85.4 s, and 37.1% of them fall in 49-53 s. This mode is a trace/scaling artifact, not tool behavior (t1_pred.py)

Previous-gap predictor over all returns with t>=2: within ±25% for 38.0%, over-estimates by more than 25% for 30.2%, p90 error +1042%. For storage-hit turns the running-median predictor under-predicts 98.8% / 99.0% (t1_pred.py)
claims.correction: Reuse is near-certain (97% of replies are followed by a next turn), so wasted prefetches of final turns are bounded at about 3%. Gap predictability is not demonstrated. Simple history predictors are poor and biased low on exactly the turns that need L3. Tool-call-based prediction is untested in these logs, and the x70 gaps come from scaled trace gaps, not real tool latencies.

result.notes:
Method. Everything was computed read-only from server.log and client.jsonl of runs 20260922_051155_three_tier_to_NAT160 and 20260922_064515_three_tier_wc_NAT160. Scratch scripts are in /tmp/claude-1001/-home-wanhr-sglang/454133c8-c6f1-4d1f-8d97-1e8cda557a0d/scratchpad/assess/: t1_load.py (parse), t1_a/b/c/d (timing components, clock check, read serialization, host-bin comparison), t1_e (fixed-window counterfactual), t1_sim.py (single-reader EDF simulation, validated against actual io_end with -0.029 s median error), t1_evict.py (L2 turnover and empirical survival curve), t1_lead.py, t1_net.py, t1_pred.py, t1_park.py, t1_bw.py, t1_ts.py, t1_q.py, t1_misc.py.

Definitions. A storage hit is a turn with cached_details.storage > 0. This includes 6 partial hits in _to with less than 50% of the prompt cached. Queue wait = load_back_init time minus (t_start + t_send); all 896 / 837 storage hits have this event. The fetch window is prefetch_start -> s2h_io. s2h_io 'tokens=' is always 0 because it is logged before the scheduler updates completed_tokens, so I used pages x 64 instead; it matches the 'prefetch success loaded=' count for every hit.

Caveats.
- The counterfactual TTFT is the observed TTFT minus (io_end - prefetch_start) plus the simulated exposed fetch. It keeps the observed post-fetch wait and the admission->first-token time.
- The simulation keeps the measured per-read IO durations and does not model the extra SSD load from re-reading evicted contexts.
- The 're-evicted' estimate applies the survival curve observed in the actual run to each parked prefetch's residency window. It assumes the parked tokens do not change eviction dynamics, but they would add 5-37% of the pool in pressure.
- One run per arm.
- The x70 gaps are trace gaps x70; 37% of them fall in 49-53 s.
- At x10/x1, storage hits are 0.1-0.2%, so Takeaway 1 only matters in this sparse regime.

Main message for the user. Takeaway 1 is worth pursuing, but the motivation needs to change. The exposed delay does not come mainly from a shallow queue that fails to hide the fetch. It comes from L3 restores that are issued reactively, run one at a time on a single thread, and arrive in bursts (58-80% of storage-hit TTFT). The SSD is idle 73-77% of the time overall but saturated in bursts.
- An early, deadline-aware prefetch works in simulation: a lead of about 10-20 s before the true arrival hides 81-100% and cuts storage-hit TTFT from 5.2-5.6 s to 0.3-1.3 s.
- It needs three things. The lead must account for the L3 backlog, not just the size/bandwidth read time. Reads must be ordered by predicted deadline. The lead must stay short enough to survive L2 turnover.
- It is fragile to gap prediction. Over-estimating the gap loses everything. Under-estimating by 50%, or using simple history predictors, loses 30-45% of the benefit to re-eviction.
- This connects to Takeaway 2: the phase with SSD congestion is the same phase with fast L2 turnover.

Code facts relevant to Takeaway 2: prefetched pages are inserted into the host tree unlocked as soon as the read completes (unified_radix_cache.py:2562-2565, 1983, 2024), and are locked only at load_back.

works.title: TokenCake: A KV-Cache-centric Serving Framework for LLM-based Multi-Agent Applications
works.mechanism: When a function call starts, it offloads the agent's KV from GPU to CPU. This only happens if the predicted stall covers a round-trip transfer and a waiting request can use the freed blocks. As the predicted completion time approaches, it gradually uploads the KV back from CPU to GPU. Upload priority mixes importance with urgency, measured as closeness to the predicted completion. An upload budget protects critical waiting requests. Tool duration is a user estimate blended with an EWMA of history.
works.difference: CPU to GPU only, with no SSD tier. Measured upload is about 32 ms for 4K tokens, while SSD fetches in the user's setup take seconds. Start time is tied to the predicted tool completion and has no queueing-delay term. The 'too early' cost is GPU blocks taken from active requests, not host-memory eviction by write-through. Load adaptation is a watermark on the GPU reservation fraction, not on prefetch timing.
evidence_quotes: "As the predicted completion time approaches, the scheduler begins a gradual upload (§4.3) to hide transfer latency behind other computation." (§4.1)

"If the upload starts only after a tool returns, the resumed request stalls on data transfer. If the upload reserves all destination GPU blocks too early, active requests lose memory before the cache is needed." (§4.3)
"Higher-priority and earlier-deadline requests are uploaded first. At each scheduling step, the scheduler computes an upload budget that protects critical waiting requests" (§4.3)
"If the tool returns earlier than predicted, the scheduler triggers an immediate upload to ensure correctness." (§4.1)
"After the first observed execution, the estimate transitions to an exponentially weighted moving average." (§4.1)
"At 4,096 tokens (256 blocks), offload takes 32.0 ms and upload takes 31.7 ms" (§7.6)

works.title: Ask the Tool, Don't Guess: Agent Tool Calls Hold Their Progress, and the Serving System Should Read It
works.mechanism: Running tools report progress, and the paper turns that into an estimate of remaining time. With a DRAM host tier (a vLLM patch), a controller 'refreshes the context one lead time before the predicted return and reloads it if it has gone'. The lead time equals the recovery budget, the time needed to get the context back. It scores triggers as timely, late (the next turn stalls) or too early (GPU memory wasted).
works.difference: Covers DRAM to GPU only, with no SSD tier and no queueing-delay term. The lead time is only the recovery budget. Its central claim is also direct evidence against T1's predictor: estimates from history or tool distributions are inaccurate. They cannot even rank long calls, and they cause early fetches that multiply reload volume.
evidence_quotes: "The recovery budget is defined as the time it takes to get a context back, and an estimator triggers when it first reports a return within that budget. The trigger is timely if it lands just enough budget before the return. Later causes the next turn to stall, while too early puts the context in GPU memory for nothing." (§4.2)
"With a host tier it adds hysteresis, letting go only once the estimate has moved well past the threshold, and refreshes the context one lead time before the predicted return." (§5.1)
"We show that no estimate fixed before a call starts can know its duration, and such estimates may not even rank the calls." (Abstract)

"With a host tier it cuts the p90 by 15 to 18%, but the estimates run out early, so the controller fetches contexts back from DRAM before they are needed, at eight to thirteen times our method's reload volume." (§5.2, on the TokenCake/CacheWise/InferCept predictors)
"The progress stream's median error at 90% of each call is under 10%, against 80% for the best history predictor" (§4.2)

works.title: Cost-Efficient Large Language Model Serving for Multi-turn Conversations with CachedAttention (AttentionStore)
works.mechanism: Scheduler-aware fetching from disk to host memory, done only for jobs already in the waiting queue. It looks at most Lpw = Cmem/Skv jobs ahead, a window set by free host capacity. Scheduler-aware eviction exempts any item inside a look-ahead eviction window of (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv jobs. It prefers to evict items near the tail of that window.
works.difference: This is T2's core idea for the disk-to-host tier: do not prefetch requests far back in the queue, and protect what the near queue needs. It bounds prefetch depth by queue position (host capacity divided by session size), not by predicted time to admission. It does not predict arrivals, so it cannot start before a request arrives. It does not model write-through of newly finished requests competing for host memory.
evidence_quotes: "If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed. The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory." (§3.3.1)
"Given the available memory capacity for prefetching Cmem and the average KV size of a session Skv, the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv." (§3.3.1)
"When CachedAttention attempts to evict one item out of AttentionStore, if finding the item to be evicted in the look-ahead eviction window, the item is exempted." (§3.3.2)

works.title: PCR: A Prefetch-Enhanced Cache Reuse System for Low-Latency RAG Serving
works.mechanism: Queue-based prefetch from SSD to DRAM for requests inside a fixed look-ahead window of the vLLM waiting queue (window size 4). A look-ahead LRU raises the priority of chunks that pending requests will reuse, protecting them from eviction.
works.difference: Uses a fixed-count window (4 requests) to avoid overfetching. It does not use a predicted time to admission and does not predict arrivals. The workload is RAG, not agent gaps.
evidence_quotes: "the prefetcher maintains a look-ahead window to identify requests within a certain range of the queue" (§4.4)
"We send the waiting requests within a preloading window (set to 4 in our configuration) to the cache engine of PCR" (§5)
"it uses scheduler-provided hints to drive prefetching within a bounded window, preventing overfetching" (§5)
"we introduce a look-ahead update mechanism that leverages pending requests from the waiting queue to predict near-future reuse and protect corresponding chunks from eviction" (§4.2)

works.title: Building py-kvcache: A Performance Characterization of External KV Caching for vLLM with NVMe SSDs (+ vLLM issue #49902 / PR #50014)
works.mechanism: Documents T2's failure mode in vLLM's tiered offload: disk-to-CPU promotions start for every waiting request, fill the CPU pool, and get evicted before use, so the request recomputes. py-kvcache's fix is a bounded lookahead with one speculative preload at a time that yields to demand loads. vLLM PR #50014 protects promotions that have landed but not been read from other promotions. Real GPU stores can still evict them.
works.difference: This is independent confirmation of T2's mechanism: speculative disk-to-host promotions for queued requests are evicted by other traffic before the request is admitted. The remedies are resource bounds and protection, not a timing rule. They do not predict when a queued request will be admitted.
evidence_quotes: "Several lookups can occur in quick succession, causing multiple promotions to reserve most of the CPU cache concurrently. Stores can then fail to obtain staging memory, and completed promotions may be evicted immediately to make room. When the request is eventually scheduled, its demand load may again find no free CPU memory and fall back to recomputing the prefix." (py-kvcache §7.3)
"In the traced run, only two requests ultimately transferred the promoted data from CPU to GPU, and a total of 3.4 TB of data was read from disk, while py-kvcache only read 85 GB" (§7.3)
"Preloading converts demand work into speculative work. It is beneficial only when the selected request is likely to execute and remains queued long enough for useful I/O to complete." (§8.1)
"The result suggests that successful preloading requires admission control and resource bounds, not merely earlier submission." (§8.1)
vLLM PR #50014: "Real GPU-driven stores are intentionally **not** gated by this — they represent confirmed demand and can still evict an unread promotion freely"

works.title: Strata: Hierarchical Context Caching for Long Context Language Model Serving (= SGLang HiCache storage prefetch; baseline)
works.mechanism: This is the behavior both takeaways criticize. When a request enters the queue and hits in storage, a prefetch from storage to host starts and overlaps the queueing delay. When the scheduler dispatches the request, any in-flight prefetch is terminated (best effort). In this repo, `_add_request_to_queue` calls `self._prefetch_kvcache(req)` and then `self.waiting_queue.append(req)` (scheduler.py:3154-3155).
works.difference: Baseline. Prefetch starts at arrival, with no prediction of when the next request comes or how long it will queue.
evidence_quotes: "the cache controller opportunistically prefetches data from storage to host memory when a cache hit is detected at the storage layer. The latency of this prefetch overlaps the request's queuing delay. Once the scheduler dispatches the request for execution, the cache controller terminates any in-flight prefetch" (§4.2.1)
scheduler.py:3154-3155: `self._prefetch_kvcache(req)` / `self.waiting_queue.append(req)`

works.title: LMCache: An Efficient KV Cache Layer for Enterprise-Scale LLM Inference
works.mechanism: Also a baseline. Once a query is admitted and waiting, its KV is prefetched from slower tiers (such as remote disk) into CPU or GPU during that wait. The connector can put a request back in the waiting queue so its I/O overlaps other work.
works.difference: Triggered at arrival or admission, like SGLang. No prediction of arrival or queueing delay, and no bound on how early to prefetch.
evidence_quotes: "if a query (with cache hit) arrives when the inference engine is processing other queries, the arriving query has to wait in queue. LMCACHE exploits this idle interval to prefetch the queued queries' KV cache from slower storage tiers into faster ones (e.g., from remote disk to local CPU memory or GPU memory)." (§5.2)

works.title: SYMPHONY: Improving Memory Management for LLM Inference Workloads
works.mechanism: Before the real request, a client sends an 'advisory request' (the schema includes "expected_arrival"). The node manager then moves the session's KV to the fastest tier available, greedily. The engine may overwrite prefetched blocks under memory pressure; lower layers get higher priority.
works.difference: Prefetch starts before arrival, but as early as possible after the advisory. No timing rule or queueing-delay term was found. The 'too early' problem is handled by letting prefetched copies be purged (a disk copy is always kept), not by delaying the fetch.
evidence_quotes: "In agent workloads, where requests are sent by preceding agents, it is possible to estimate a minimum arrival time." (§3.3)

"the SYMPHONY node manager greedily transfers the K,V cache to occupy available GPU memory whenever it is free. However, under increased memory pressure, the underlying serving library can overwrite this memory by purging parts of the K,V cache." (§3.3)

"Based on the current free GPU memory, the system decides to prefetch the K,V cache for Session ID: 2 onto the GPU in anticipation of the actual inference request. However, as the inference for Session ID: 1 continues, the size of its K,V cache grows, eventually consuming all available GPU memory." (§3.3)

works.title: KVFlow: Efficient Prefix Caching for Accelerating LLM-Based Multi-Agent Workflows
works.mechanism: While the current agent runs, it prefetches from CPU to GPU the KV of agents the Step Graph predicts will run next, with a limit on concurrent prefetches. Status-aware scheduling skips requests whose KV is still loading.
works.difference: Lead time is counted in workflow steps, not predicted wall-clock time. CPU to GPU only. It admits that prefetch can be late under high concurrency but does not adjust timing for it.
evidence_quotes: "while Planner is executing, the system anticipates that Executor 1 will be invoked next and proactively prefetches its KV cache from CPU to GPU." (§3.2)

"When the current agent's execution time is shorter than the prefetch duration, generation may still be blocked by incomplete KV loading. This is common in high-concurrency settings, where multiple workflows compete for CPU-GPU bandwidth and cause queuing delays." (§3.2)

works.title: PBKV: Efficient Serving for Dynamic Agent Workflows with Prediction-based KV-Cache Management
works.mechanism: Built on SGLang HiCache. Prefetch from host to GPU is deliberately conservative: it only fills free or retired GPU space, never evicts active cache, runs only on pure-decode batches, and looks only one step ahead.
works.difference: Applies the 'do no harm' limit on how early to prefetch (never displace valuable cache) at the host-to-GPU tier, using step-count prediction. No wall-clock timing, no queueing-delay term, no SSD tier.
evidence_quotes: "we do not evict any active cache to make room for prefetched data" (§4.3)
"We deliberately restrict ranking to the one-step horizon because prefetching is naturally incremental: a node that will be reused two steps ahead can simply be fetched at the next step." (§4.3)

works.title: Learning Agent Execution for KV-Cache Management in Agentic Serving (CacheScout)
works.mechanism: Learns agent-transition probabilities online. Between steps, it sends a warmup request that rebuilds the likely next agent's shared anchor (system prompt and tools). A predictability threshold gates this. Its related work names a line of systems that reload the paused agent's KV from CPU just before the tool returns.
works.difference: Prefetch is a recompute warmup of shared prefixes across sessions, not restoration of a session's private context from a tier. No timing model.
evidence_quotes: "Another line of work fills the tool pause with other agents' work and reloads the paused agent's KV from CPU just before the tool returns [4, 24, 39]." (§6; [4]=TokenCake)
"Proactive prefetching is beneficial only when execution is sufficiently predictable." (§3.4)
"On its own, prefetch is inert on these workloads" (§5)

works.title: Continuum: Efficient and Robust Multi-Turn LLM Agent Scheduling with KV Cache Time-to-Live
works.mechanism: Pins the KV of a tool-calling request in GPU for a TTL. The TTL maximizes P(return within τ) × benefit − cost. The benefit includes reload/prefill cost and the queueing delay the request avoids. P comes from an empirical CDF of past tool durations, and queueing delay is a sliding-window average.
works.difference: Uses the same two predicted inputs T1/T2 propose (a tool-return distribution and queueing delay), but to decide how long to keep KV in GPU, not when to start a prefetch. It assumes a permanently backlogged queue.
evidence_quotes: "we estimate P(τ,f) using the empirical CDF derived from historical tool-call records S[f]" (§4)
"Continuum selectively pins the KV cache in GPU memory with a time-to-live value determined by the reload cost and potential queueing delay induced by eviction." (Abstract)
"We assume that the waiting queue always contains enough requests for this blocking effect to occur when KV retention is necessary." (§4)

works.title: Adaptive KV Retention for LLM Agents at Human-Approval Timescales
works.mechanism: A tiered retention controller that offloads to host when a request suspends. Host-memory policy switches by regime: below λcrit = C2/Wref (from Little's law), host copies are free to keep. Above it, host residency has a price and host copies expire after a load-dependent t2(λ).
works.difference: A load-regime-adaptive host residency budget, which is the 'residency/protection budget' ingredient. It governs retention, not prefetch start time, and has no SSD tier.
evidence_quotes: "Uncongested regime. When host DRAM has spare capacity, α2 = α3 = 0" / "Congested regime. Once host DRAM becomes scarce, retaining a host copy imposes an opportunity cost on other suspended contexts." (§3)
"By Little's law, host saturation occurs at λcrit = C2/Wref." (§3.3)
"This yields a load-indexed host expiration policy, cpu_ttl(λ), which discards host-resident KV after t2(λ)." (§3.3)

works.title: Idleness is Relative: Exploiting Tool-Call Idle Windows for Offloading in Agentic Systems with MORI
works.mechanism: Ranks programs by how idle they are and places them in GPU, CPU or a waiting queue, with admission control for each tier. A CPU-resident program is promoted to GPU only after its tool call completes.
works.difference: Covers tier residency and admission control, but reload happens on return, not before. No timing rule.
evidence_quotes: "MORI ranks all active programs by idleness, assigns the busiest to GPU HBM and the most idle to CPU DRAM, dynamically shifts the partition boundary to match hardware capacity, and enforces admission control at each memory tier." (Abstract)
"When GPU capacity becomes available, the scheduler promotes programs in a priority order: (1) CPU-queue programs that have completed their tool call and are waiting for inference" (§4.3.1)

works.title: UNISON: A Co-Designed Near-Memory Scheduler of Session KV Residency for LLM Agents
works.mechanism: At the start of a gap, TIDE sets a migration budget of (estimated remaining gap × DMA bandwidth). It migrates sessions between SRAM and HBM so the right residents are in the fast tier when the next request arrives.
works.difference: A hardware SRAM/HBM scheduler. Migration starts as soon as the gap begins, bounded by the gap, rather than just in time. No queueing delay.
evidence_quotes: "On a gap_start event with estimated remaining duration ∆, the migration budget in tokens is B= ∆·B" (§III-C)
"TIDE converts this idle window into a DMA budget and migrates sessions between SRAM and HBM so that the lowest-scoring residents occupy the fast tier when the next request arrives." (§III-C)

works.title: SGLang RFC #27574 'Programmatic KV Cache for Agentic Workloads' and RFC #36224 'First-Class, Versioned KV Hint Envelope'
works.mechanism: Proposes router-initiated hints: Share, Prefetch, Demote and Pin. 'Prefetch' means moving KV to a hotter tier before it is needed, but the RFC leaves it as a TODO. The shipped kv.prefetch@1.0 action acts only on the current request. Pre-arrival transfer is listed as a non-goal.
works.difference: Upstream SGLang names T1's concept but has no timing rule. It explicitly defers pre-arrival scheduling and admission semantics, which leaves exactly this gap open in the engine.
evidence_quotes: #27574: "Move KV into a hotter tier *before* it is needed: warm GPU for a likely next-turn prefix"
#27574: "TODO - measure request-time L3 restoration before adding proactive Prefetch or Demote execution APIs"
#36224 Non-goals: "Adding proactive pre-arrival transfer semantics before their scheduling, admission, and telemetry requirements are specified."
#36224: "`kv.prefetch@1.0` | Request normal SGLang storage restoration for the current request, including below the usual prefetch threshold."

works.title: llm-d blog: Pull, Don't Recompute: Peer-to-Peer KV Cache Sharing in llm-d
works.mechanism: Lists 'prefetch ahead of arrival' from CPU as planned future work.
works.difference: Planned, not implemented. No timing rule.
evidence_quotes: "Prefetch ahead of arrival. Trigger the pull from local or remote CPU when a session's next request is predictable, so the transfer overlaps idle time instead of the request's critical path."

works.title: Where Should the KV Cache Live? Placement Policies Across GPU, CPU, and SSD for Long-Lived Sessions
works.mechanism: A discrete-event simulator of GPU, CPU and SSD tiers that sweeps prefetch lookahead against placement policies.
works.difference: A cautionary data point: in its simulated setting (batch one), prefetch did not pay for its bandwidth, even with an oracle. It does not model queueing.
evidence_quotes: "prefetch as recommended does not pay for its bandwidth: across a policy×cache-size grid, even a future-reading oracle beats no-prefetch in none of the cells." (Abstract)

works.title: Informed Prefetching and Caching (TIP)
works.mechanism: Classic theory. Weighs the benefit of prefetching (less stall) against the cost of the buffers it takes. The prefetch horizon P(T_CPU) = T_disk/(T_CPU+T_hit+T_driver) is the distance beyond which prefetching gains nothing, so it caps the buffers used for prefetching.
works.difference: Theoretical basis for T2: prefetching earlier than the horizon only uses up cache. For KV tiers, the horizon becomes (fetch time) measured against the predicted time until admission, not a count of accesses.
evidence_quotes: "There is no benefit from prefetching further ahead than the prefetch horizon." (Fig. 4 caption)

"Because there is no benefit from prefetching more deeply than the prefetch horizon, we can easily bound the impact of informed prefetching on effective cache size; prefetching a stream of hints will not lead informed prefetching to acquire more than P(TCPU) buffers." (§4.2)
"applies cost-benefit analysis to allocate buffers where they will have the greatest impact" (Abstract)

works.title: A Study of Integrated Prefetching and Caching Strategies
works.mechanism: Sets out four rules any optimal integrated prefetching and caching strategy must follow: optimal prefetching, optimal replacement, do no harm, and first opportunity. Compares 'aggressive' and 'conservative' strategies.
works.difference: Theory behind T2's claim that prefetching too early causes eviction. Starting a prefetch reserves a cache slot early, and 'Do No Harm' forbids prefetching something that displaces data needed sooner. In the x10/x1 regime, host space taken for a request far back in the queue competes with write-through of finished turns and with requests admitted sooner.
evidence_quotes: "prefetching file blocks into a cache can be harmful even if the blocks will be accessed in the near future. This is because a cache block needs to be reserved for the block being prefetched at the time the prefetch is initiated." (§1)
"Rule 3: Do No Harm Never discard block A to prefetch block B when A will be referenced before B." (§2.2)
"aggressive prefetching is a double-edged sword: it hides fetch latency, but it may increase the number of fetches." (§1.1)

works.title: A Trace-Driven Comparison of Algorithms for Parallel Prefetching and Caching
works.venue_year: OSDI 1996 (Kimbrel, Tomkins, Patterson, Bershad, Cao, Felten, Gibson, Karlin, Li)
works.mechanism: 'Fixed horizon' issues each fetch as late as possible so it completes just in time. 'Forestall' estimates the point at which it must start prefetching to avoid a stall. It behaves like aggressive when fetches are backlogged and like fixed horizon otherwise.
works.difference: The closest classic analogue of the combined formulation: one just-in-time rule that adapts to the regime. It lacks the LLM-specific parts: predicted arrival from tool gaps, a queueing-delay term for admission, multiple tiers (SSD to host), and write-through contention.
evidence_quotes: "a block prefetched too early reduces the effectiveness of the cache, while a block cached too long reduces the effectiveness of prefetching." (Abstract; PDF text, spacing normalized)

"Fixed horizon tries to fetch as late as possible without stalling in order to make the best possible replacement decision. Each fetch is issued so that it will complete just in time for the reference." (§2.3)
"Forestall tries to avoid stalling while still making good (late) replacement decisions by estimating the point at which it needs to begin prefetching in order to prevent stalling." (§5)

"aggressive prefetching helps to alleviate the problem; that more conservative prefetching is appropriate when significant I/O stalls are not present; and that a single, simple strategy is capable of doing both." (Abstract)

works.title: Feedback Directed Prefetching: Improving the Performance and Bandwidth-Efficiency of Hardware Prefetchers
works.mechanism: Measures prefetch accuracy, lateness and prefetcher-caused cache pollution at run time, and adjusts prefetch aggressiveness (distance/degree) from that feedback.
works.difference: A hardware analogue of adjusting prefetch timing from measured lateness (T1's failure) and pollution (T2's failure). The same two metrics could be logged per turn in HiCache.
evidence_quotes: "A prefetch is defined to be late if the prefetched data has not yet returned from main memory by the time a load or store instruction requests the prefetched data." (§2.2.2)
"If the prefetcher-generated cache pollution is high, the performance of the processor can degrade because useful data in the cache could be evicted by prefetched data." (§2.2.3)
"Aggressive prefetching reduces the lateness of prefetches because an aggressive prefetcher generates prefetch requests earlier than a conservative one would." (§2.2.2)

result.novelty_assessment:
Each takeaway on its own has close prior work. The single rule that joins them was not found in the LLM-serving literature I read, and a classic storage algorithm already has the same regime-adaptive shape.

Coverage: web search, then about 30 papers read from their full text, plus the relevant SGLang, vLLM, Mooncake and Dynamo RFCs and PRs. "Not found" means not found in this set, not proof that nothing exists.

**Takeaway 1 (start the prefetch during the tool gap, before the next turn arrives): substantial prior work.**
- TokenCake (EuroSys '27) uploads offloaded KV from CPU to GPU "as the predicted completion time approaches". It frames the same too-late versus too-early tension.
- Ask the Tool, Don't Guess (arXiv 2609.18849, 16 Sep 2026) "refreshes the context one lead time before the predicted return" from DRAM. It scores triggers as timely, late or too early.
- SYMPHONY (advisory requests carrying an expected_arrival field), KVFlow (next-step prefetch) and UNISON (gap-start migration budget) also move KV before arrival.
- SGLang's own RFC #27574 names a pre-arrival "Prefetch" hint as a TODO. RFC #36224 lists "proactive pre-arrival transfer semantics" as a non-goal. The llm-d blog lists "prefetch ahead of arrival" as future work.

What T1 could still add:
- **SSD-to-host tier.** All of the above target CPU-to-GPU or on-chip tiers, where a fetch takes tens of ms (TokenCake measured 31.7 ms for 4K tokens). In the user's setup a 35K-token context is 35,000 × 98,304 B ≈ 3.2 GiB, about 1.7 s at 1.88 GiB/s. Earlier runs measured SSD restores at 2.6–3.3 s p50. At that scale, lead-time accuracy matters far more.
- **Queueing-delay term.** None of these systems adds predicted queueing delay to the start time.

Main risk to T1: Ask the Tool shows that predictors fixed before a call (tool name or history) have about 80% median error near the end of the call and cannot rank long calls. That error made the tested controllers fetch contexts back from DRAM before they were needed, at 8–13× the progress method's reload volume. T1's "estimated tool-return distribution" is exactly that kind of predictor. The replayed-trace benchmark (gap = trace gap × scale) gives it more predictability than real tools would.

**Takeaway 2 (under deep queues, delay the prefetch until shortly before admission so it is not evicted): substantial prior work.**
- CachedAttention (ATC'24) prefetches from disk to host only within a look-ahead window of Lpw = Cmem/Skv waiting jobs, and exempts that window from eviction.
- PCR uses a fixed 4-request window "preventing overfetching".
- py-kvcache (Sep 2026) and vLLM #49902/#50014 document the same failure in vLLM: promotions for queued requests are evicted before use and the request recomputes. PR #50014 lets real GPU stores still evict unread promotions, which is analogous to write-through pressure in HiCache. py-kvcache concludes that preloading "requires admission control and resource bounds, not merely earlier submission".

What T2 could still add: the prior remedies are count or capacity windows, protection, and bounded concurrency. None found times the start by a predicted time to admission, and none found ties it to write-through of finished turns in a write-through host tier.

**The combined formulation.** The rule is: start time = predicted arrival (from the tool-gap distribution) + predicted queueing delay − predicted fetch time − margin, under a host residency budget. With a shallow queue this starts before arrival (T1). With a deep queue it starts shortly before admission (T2).
- Not found in LLM serving. Continuum uses both predicted inputs, a tool-duration CDF and a sliding-window queueing delay, but only to set a GPU retention TTL, not a prefetch start time. The human-approval retention paper (arXiv 2608.30830) makes host residency regime-adaptive via Little's law, but for retention only.
- The idea has direct classic ancestors. Kimbrel et al. (OSDI'96) have "fixed horizon" (fetch so it completes just in time) and "forestall" (estimate the point at which prefetching must begin, behaving aggressively when fetches are backlogged). They show "a single, simple strategy is capable of doing both". TIP's prefetch horizon (SOSP'95) and Cao et al.'s "Do No Harm" rule (SIGMETRICS'95) explain why prefetching past the horizon only wastes cache.

**Verdict.** Both takeaways are legitimate and well motivated, and they are two regimes of one timing rule. As separate ideas they are incremental over TokenCake / Ask the Tool (T1) and CachedAttention / PCR / py-kvcache (T2). A defensible contribution would be the unified rule applied to the SSD-to-host tier, framed as "forestall for agentic KV tiers". It needs:
- a predictor for admission time, not just arrival time;
- a host residency budget that accounts for write-through of finished requests;
- measured evidence of both failure modes in one system: T1's stall at x70 (SSD restores 2.6–3.3 s p50 with near-zero queueing) and T2's eviction at x10/x1.

Reviewers will ask how robust it is to tool-duration prediction error, which the Ask the Tool paper shows is large.

works.title: Cost-Efficient LLM Serving for Multi-turn Conversations with CachedAttention (AttentionStore)
works.mechanism: Three tiers: HBM, host DRAM, disk. Session KV is saved to host memory asynchronously while the turn runs. 'Scheduler-aware fetching': a look-ahead window over the job queue promotes disk-resident KV to DRAM before a queued job runs. The window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv, i.e. as many queued jobs as host memory can hold, so only jobs near the head are fetched. 'Scheduler-aware eviction': KV whose job is inside a longer eviction window ((Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv) is exempt from eviction, and DRAM-to-disk eviction takes items near the tail of that window first. The unit is a whole session. Nothing happens before a request arrives, since arrivals are treated as random.
works.difference: This is T2's core idea, published in 2024: fetch from disk only for jobs close to execution, and do not evict KV that queued jobs will use. The window is set by queue position and host capacity, not by predicted admission time. There is no queue-delay or SSD-bandwidth model, no prefix tree or shared prefixes (whole-session items), no link between host copies and device residency, no agent or tool signals, and no switching by load level. The evaluation uses ShareGPT with Poisson arrivals. What T2 could still add: a lead time in seconds (predicted admission time minus fetch time), protection of prefixes already matched in host memory at arrival (not only prefetched ones), and page-granular trees with a shared system prompt.
evidence_quotes: §3.3.1: "CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed. If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed."
§3.3.1: "The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory. ... the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv."

§3.3.2: "When CachedAttention attempts to evict one item out of AttentionStore, if finding the item to be evicted in the look-ahead eviction window, the item is exempted. When CachedAttention evicts one item from the host memory to disks, the item located at the tail of the look-ahead eviction window has a higher priority to be evicted."

works.title: SGLang HiCache (docs, LMSYS blog, and the local code used in campaigns 7-9)
works.venue_year: LMSYS blog 2025-09-10; docs and code as of 2026
works.mechanism: After L1/L2 matching, a request whose remaining span is at least 256 tokens gets an L3 query and prefetch when it enters the waiting queue. Termination is best_effort, wait_complete or timeout. The prefetch is finalised only when the FCFS admission scan reaches the request. The host anchor is protected (protect_host) only while a prefetch is outstanding. If the span is under the threshold, or the L3 hit is under the threshold, the lock is never taken or is released immediately. A prefetch that allocates host pages calls evict_host at arrival time. evict_host only evicts nodes that are no longer on the device.

Staged L3 pages sit outside the tree until finalisation, and upstream issue #32724 says they stay pinned. What is left unprotected while queued is the prefix that was matched in host memory at arrival, whenever no prefetch is outstanding. That fits the reported observation that 87% of recomputes had a <1K-token unmatched tail. An arrival-time prefetch for a request deep in the queue can also evict other queued requests' prefixes.
