result.novelty_assessment:
Short answer: Takeaway 2 on its own is already published. Takeaway 1's idea is published for the host-memory tier and announced, but not built, for the SSD tier. What is left for a paper is narrower than either takeaway: one prefetch policy that times the SSD fetch to a request's predicted admission, with tests showing when it helps.

**Takeaway 2 (fetch later, just before admission, and protect queued requests' KV)**
- **Core idea: already published.** CachedAttention/AttentionStore (USENIX ATC 2024) does both halves:
  - It fetches from disk only for jobs near the head of the queue. The look-ahead window is sized to what host memory can hold: "Lpw = Cmem/Skv".
  - It protects queued work from eviction: "if finding the item to be evicted in the look-ahead eviction window, the item is exempted". When moving KV from host memory to disk, it evicts items near the tail of the window first.
- **Deployed engines already cover parts of it:**
  - vLLM's connector lookup only runs when the admission scan reaches a request (scheduler.py:859/937/1222), and the LMCache adapter pins what it finds until the request is scheduled (vllm_v1_adapter.py:1377-1378).
  - Upstream SGLang merged a reactive fix in September 2026 (PRs #39283 and #40042, function `_prefetch_after_device_hit_loss`). At admission it re-issues the L3 lookup for a range that "shrank before admission". This fix is not in the local fork used for campaigns 7-9. PR #40011 describes the problem as "the device match evicts while the request is queued".
- **What could still be new is incremental:**
  - a lead time measured in seconds (predicted admission time minus SSD fetch time at 1.88 GiB/s), instead of CachedAttention's window counted in jobs;
  - page-level radix trees where a host copy cannot be evicted while the node is on the GPU;
  - protecting prefixes matched in host memory at arrival, not only prefetched ones;
  - switching behaviour with load.
- **The mechanism is worded inaccurately for SGLang.** Staged L3-to-host pages are held outside the tree until the admission scan finalises them; issue #32724 says they stay "pinned longer than necessary". What is actually left unprotected while a request waits is its host-memory match from arrival:
  - hiradix_cache.py:1792/1797 returns without `protect_host` when the remaining span is under 256 tokens;
  - lines 621-623 revoke the prefetch and release the host lock when the L3 hit is under 256 tokens;
  - line 632 lets an arrival-time prefetch evict other requests' host copies;
  - line 1367 skips host copies of nodes still on the GPU (this is the "lock status" coupling in Takeaway 2).

  This fits the reported 87% of recomputes that had a <1K-token unmatched tail. Takeaway 2 should be reframed as admission-aware protection plus just-in-time staging, with CachedAttention cited as the source of the idea.

**Takeaway 1 (start the fetch before the next turn arrives, using predicted tool-return time)**
- **Published for host memory to GPU:**
  - TokenCake (arXiv 2510.18586) starts a gradual upload "as the predicted completion time approaches", using a per-tool EWMA predictor. It also states the too-late versus too-early tension that Takeaways 1 and 2 split between them.
  - KVFlow (NeurIPS 2025, built on SGLang HiCache) and PBKV prefetch for the predicted next step.
  - "Ask the Tool" (arXiv 2609.18849, SWE-agent replays) refreshes or reloads "one lead time before the predicted return". It also finds that fetching back too early costs 8-13x the reload volume.
  - Continuum uses exactly Takeaway 1's inputs (a tool-duration distribution plus per-turn queueing delay, computed at request end), but to set how long KV stays pinned in GPU, not to prefetch.
- **Announced but not built for storage to GPU:**
  - NVIDIA Dynamo (April 2026) calls prefetch "the missing piece" and says it is "building prefetch hooks" to bring "blocks from storage to GPU ahead of the next request".
  - SGLang RFC #27574 lists Prefetch ("warm GPU for a likely next-turn prefix") as a TODO.
- **Counter-evidence:** a simulation paper (arXiv 2609.16215) finds speculative prefetch does not pay on a contended link. At 1.88 GiB/s the SSD is exactly that kind of link.

**What is defensible**
A single prefetch start time:

  start = end of turn + predicted tool return + predicted queue wait − SSD fetch time

The policy would:
- only hold staged KV in a bounded, protected host budget;
- move smoothly from early fetching when load is light (Takeaway 1) to fetching at admission when load is heavy (Takeaway 2);
- be measured on real SWE traces across the x70/x10/x1 gap scales.

I found no source that combines the SSD tier, a queue-wait term and host-memory-aware protection. The contribution would be that combination, the policy, and the measurement that arrival-time prefetch (Strata, HiCache, LMCache) fails in both regimes. It is not the idea of starting early or late.

**Risks to check before building**
- At x10 and x1 all host-memory arms performed the same and storage hits were only 0.1-0.2%. The paper must show that recomputes come from timing and protection, not from the live set simply exceeding the host pool; otherwise better timing buys little.
- Competing remedies need to be baselines: Cake (compute and load a request's KV in parallel) and upstream SGLang's reactive re-fetch at admission.

works.title: TokenCake: A KV-Cache-centric Serving Framework for LLM-based Multi-Agent Applications
works.venue_year: arXiv 2510.18586 (v1 Oct 2025, v3 2026); repo README says accepted to EuroSys '27
works.mechanism: Tiers: GPU and CPU only. When a function call starts, a gate decides whether to offload the agent's KV to CPU DRAM, and only if the predicted stall is longer than the round-trip transfer. Signal: a per-function-type time estimate that blends a user-supplied value from the graph definition with an EWMA of observed durations (Eq. 1). Start time: 'as the predicted completion time approaches', uploads are ranked by importance plus urgency (closeness to the predicted completion) and GPU blocks are reserved gradually, at most half the remaining deficit per step. If the tool returns early, an immediate upload is triggered.
works.difference: This is the same core mechanism as T1: restore during the tool gap, timed by a predicted return. But it is 2-tier (GPU to CPU, 100 GB CPU pool, about 32 ms to upload 4K tokens), with no SSD-to-host stage. It has no queueing-delay term: the window is T_FC - T_transfer, and the agent 'resumes immediately' once uploaded. There is no regime adaptivity. Its gradual reservation addresses a T2-like 'too early' cost, but only in GPU memory. The released code has not implemented predictive prefetch yet.
evidence_quotes: "TokenCake's Temporal Scheduler employs an event-driven, opportunistic policy to proactively offload idle KV Caches during function calls and uses predictive uploading to hide data transfer latency." (abstract)

"If the policy approves, the KV Cache is transferred to CPU memory asynchronously. As the predicted completion time approaches, the scheduler begins a gradual upload (§4.3) to hide transfer latency behind other computation." (§4.1)

"The scheduler maintains a per-function-type time estimate. When no history is available, the estimate defaults to the value supplied by the user through the graph definition, or to a conservative system-wide constant if no user estimate exists. After the first observed execution, the estimate transitions to an exponentially weighted moving average." (§4.1)
"The scheduler computes the available scheduling window as the predicted stall minus the transfer overhead: T_window = T_FC − T_transfer." (§4.2)

"If the upload starts only after a tool returns, the resumed request stalls on data transfer. If the upload reserves all destination GPU blocks too early, active requests lose memory before the cache is needed." (§4.3)
"All configurations reserve 100 GB of CPU memory as the offload destination."; "At 4,096 tokens (256 blocks), offload takes 32.0 ms and upload takes 31.7 ms"
"At noise 0.25, TokenCake regresses by 8.3% because mistimed uploads pass the gate's feasibility check but still cause harmful migrations." (§7.5)

README (github.com/pku-lemonade/TokenCake): "The current implementation uses vLLM v0.22.0 and performs event-driven preservation with demand-triggered CPU-to-GPU recovery; predictive prefetching and further policy tuning remain active development work."

works.title: Ask the Tool, Don't Guess: Agent Tool Calls Hold Their Progress, and the Serving System Should Read It
works.mechanism: Tiers: HBM only, or HBM + DRAM (vLLM's own offloading); no SSD. Signal: live progress the running tool reports (fraction remaining, or a near-end marker), converted linearly to a remaining-time estimate. Start time: a controller keeps (refreshes) a context while the remaining time is under a threshold. It lets the context go to the host with hysteresis, and 'refreshes the context one lead time before the predicted return and reloads it if it has gone'. The lead time is the 'recovery budget', the time needed to get the context back (0.5 s and 2 s budgets are evaluated).
works.difference: This is the same 'reload one lead time before predicted return' mechanism, but DRAM to HBM only. The lead time is transfer time, not transfer plus expected queue wait. The paper directly argues against T1's proposed signal (a history-based tool-return distribution): history predictors are rarely timely near the end of a call. The 'too early wastes memory' framing is T2-like, but queue depth is not modeled.
evidence_quotes: "Serving systems decide whether that cache stays, leaves, or comes back by guessing how long the tool will run, from the tool's name, its history, a duration declared before the call, or the engine's own occupancy." (abstract)
"We replay the agent sessions of Section 4 across all methods on a 4×H100 SXM instance in two configurations: GPU memory only, and GPU memory with DRAM as an offload tier." (§5.1)

"Our method based on progress keeps a context while the reported remaining time is under a threshold. With a host tier it adds hysteresis, letting go only once the estimate has moved well past the threshold, and refreshes the context one lead time before the predicted return." (§5.1)
"With a host tier, the controller also refreshes the context one lead time before the predicted return and reloads it if it has gone." (App. D)

"The recovery budget is defined as the time it takes to get a context back, and an estimator triggers when it first reports a return within that budget. The trigger is timely if it lands just enough budget before the return. Later causes the next turn to stall, while too early puts the context in GPU memory for nothing." (§4.2)
"the progress stream triggers in time in 31 % of test runs, 15 % of builds and 50 % of scripts; the best baseline in 0, 0 and 13 %." (appendix figure caption)

"With a host tier it cuts the p90 by 15 to 18%, but the estimates run out early, so the controller fetches contexts back from DRAM before they are needed, at eight to thirteen times our method's reload volume." (§5.2, on history predictors)

works.title: SGLang RFC #27574 'Programmatic KV Cache for Agentic Workloads' (plus #21846 roadmap, #36224 KV hint envelope)
works.venue_year: GitHub RFC, opened 2026-06-08 (#36224 opened 2026-08-24); open, not implemented
works.mechanism: Tiers: L1 GPU / L2 host / L3 Mooncake shared storage. Proposes router-initiated hints. 'Prefetch' means moving KV to a hotter tier before the continuation arrives (L3 to host to GPU). 'Demote' is paired with 'Prefetch': KV offloaded during a pause is warmed back before resume. Signal: the orchestrator knows 'which tool gap is 10ms vs 10min'. Start time: not specified. Proactive Prefetch is explicitly deferred until request-time L3 restoration has been measured. The #36224 kv.prefetch action only restores for the current request.
works.difference: This is the same idea, including the SSD/L3 tier, in the user's own engine. It is only a proposal: no timing rule, no predictor, no queue-delay term, no evaluation. The only implemented piece is L3 Pin via a Mooncake TTL lease. The RFC's TODO asks for exactly the measurement the user's campaigns provide.
evidence_quotes: "Prefetch: Move KV into a hotter tier *before* it is needed: warm GPU for a likely next-turn prefix; pull shared KV into a freshly selected worker; reload main-agent KV during a subagent's close."
"Demote moves together with Prefetch/Onboard - the KV offloaded during a pause is the KV warmed back before the continuation resumes."
"TODO - measure request-time L3 restoration before adding proactive Prefetch or Demote execution APIs"
"The orchestrator knows the structure request-local policy cannot: which sessions are live, which token ranges are shared prefixes vs unique tails, which tool gap is 10ms vs 10min"
#36224: "`kv.prefetch@1.0` | Request normal SGLang storage restoration for the current request, including below the usual prefetch threshold."

#21846 Q3 roadmap (unchecked item): "Build a KV cache orchestrator across the router and engine to detect agentic workflows—including sessions, sub-agents, and tool calls—and provide scheduling hints such as `PREFETCH`, `DEMOTE`, and `PIN`"

works.title: KVFlow: Efficient Prefix Caching for Accelerating LLM-Based Multi-Agent Workflows
works.mechanism: Tiers: GPU plus CPU secondary cache, built on SGLang v0.4.4's hierarchical radix cache; no SSD. Signal: an Agent Step Graph gives each agent a steps-to-execution value. Start time: while the current agent is executing, the fixed-prompt KV of the agents scheduled in the next step is prefetched CPU to GPU in background threads, if evictable GPU memory is large enough. Status-aware scheduling skips requests whose KV is still loading.
works.difference: The prefetch starts before the request arrives, but it is triggered by the workflow step, with no wall-clock prediction of tool return. It covers only shared agent fixed prompts, not per-session private context, and only CPU to GPU. It explicitly treats tool-duration handling (InferCept) as orthogonal. Its steps-to-execution eviction protects soon-needed entries, which is T2-adjacent, but it has no queue-delay model.
evidence_quotes: "KVFlow introduces a fully overlapped KV prefetching mechanism, which proactively loads required tensors from CPU to GPU in background threads for agents scheduled in the next step, thereby avoiding cache miss stalls during generation." (abstract)
"while Planner is executing, the system anticipates that Executor 1 will be invoked next and proactively prefetches its KV cache from CPU to GPU." (§3.2)

"When the current agent's execution time is shorter than the prefetch duration, generation may still be blocked by incomplete KV loading. This is common in high-concurrency settings, where multiple workflows compete for CPU-GPU bandwidth and cause queuing delays." (§3.2)
"the backend can update eviction priorities in the KV cache tree accordingly and trigger prefetching if the evictable GPU memory is large enough." (§3.3)

"InferCept [34] predicts tool calling durations and uses a cost model to decide whether to retain, swap, or discard the KV cache of intercepted requests. These optimizations are orthogonal to KVFlow" (related work)

works.title: Continuum (a.k.a. CacheTTL): Efficient and Robust Multi-Turn LLM Agent Scheduling with KV Cache Time-to-Live
works.venue_year: arXiv 2511.02230 (v1 Nov 2025, v7 Sep 2026); venue not found
works.mechanism: Tiers: pins KV in GPU for a TTL during a tool call. CPU DRAM and SSD offload via LMCache are used as substrates and baselines, and a reload happens on demand when the next turn is scheduled. Signal: a per-tool empirical CDF of past durations, P(τ,f), plus a sliding-window average of the queueing delay that evicted requests experience. Start time: no prefetch. The TTL is chosen as argmax_τ P(τ,f)·(T·η + Prefill-Reload) − τ.
works.difference: It uses the same signal T1 proposes (a tool-return distribution) and an explicit queueing-delay estimate, but for retention in GPU, not to time a prefetch from a lower tier. It states that even a CPU-reloadable context still waits in the queue, which supports the premise of T1 and T2. No pre-arrival fetch from CPU or SSD is performed.
evidence_quotes: "If the KV cache was evicted for this step, the engine must recompute the prefix (prefill) or reload from CPU (if CPU offloading is enabled [14]) when the tool execution completes and the next inference step begins."

"When the next inference step has its KV cache evicted from GPU memory, even if the KV cache can be reloaded from CPU, it will also have to wait in the waiting queue for other requests to free up GPU memory before starting inference."

"T can be estimated as the sliding window average for queueing delay experienced by requests who was evicted. Since we cannot fully predict the duration of the next tool call, we estimate P(τ,f) using the empirical CDF derived from historical tool-call records S[f]."
"Figure 15: Continnum reduces delay when we extend offloading devices to SSDs beyond CPU offloading."

works.title: InferCept: Efficient Intercept Support for Augmented Large Language Model Inference
works.mechanism: Tiers: GPU and CPU swap. For each interception it chooses preserve, discard or swap by minimizing estimated GPU memory waste, and swaps out in pipelined chunks. Signal: an interception duration that is profiled offline or estimated dynamically as T_INT = t_now − t_call. Start time: swap-in is reactive. Resumed requests enter a swap queue and are swapped in FCFS under a per-iteration budget after the interception returns.
works.difference: It shares only the signal class (a duration estimate) and GPU-to-CPU offload during the gap. It does not prefetch before the interception ends and has no SSD tier. The duration estimate drives the preserve/discard/swap choice, not the restore time.
evidence_quotes: "possible approach to handle interceptions is to swap contexts to CPU memory when an interception happens (we call it Swap)."

"INFERCEPT maintains three queues: a running queue containing currently running requests in the system, a swap queue containing requests that have been resumed but are previously swapped out during the interception, and a waiting queue." (§4.3)
"we propose a dynamic estimation method by setting T̂_INT = t_now − t_call where t_now is the current time updated each iteration and t_call is when the last interception was initiated." (§4.4)

works.title: Autellix: An Efficient Serving Engine for LLM Agents as General Programs
works.venue_year: arXiv 2502.13965 (2025); venue not found on the arXiv page
works.mechanism: Program-level scheduling that preempts and prioritizes LLM calls by each program's completed service. GPU-CPU swapping serves preemption only. The time of the last call completion is tracked only to detect long external interrupts. No KV handling specific to tool gaps and no prefetch was found.
works.difference: It schedules calls; it does not place KV across tiers during tool gaps. CacheScout cites it as reloading 'just before the tool returns', but that is not found in the Autellix text.
evidence_quotes: "Most recent call completion: The last time an LLM call finished—used for detecting long external interrupts."

"With preemptive scheduling, LLM engines must handle a large volume of concurrent LLM calls, leading to frequent GPU-CPU transfers as KV-cache blocks are repeatedly swapped to serve different requests"

works.title: Parrot: Efficient Serving of LLM-based Applications with Semantic Variable
works.mechanism: GPU-only context management (Fill, Generate, FreeContext, context fork) with DAG-aware scheduling. Native function calls run on the client. No tiering and no prefetch.
works.difference: No tool-gap KV handling, no lower tier and no timing.
evidence_quotes: "Currently, Parrot only supports cloud-side orchestration of LLM requests without involving dynamic control flow and native functions (e.g., Python Code). They still require client-side execution."
"The FreeContext method explicitly frees a context (i.e. free its KV cache in GPU memory)."

works.title: SAGA: Workflow-Atomic Scheduling for AI Agent Inference on GPU Clusters
works.mechanism: HBM retention with a tool-call-aware TTL (per-tool EMA latency distribution, p95). Speculative prefetch starts when a node finishes inference and begins tool execution: the prefix KV of the most likely successor is loaded into spare GPU memory. CPU/DRAM swap is explicitly left to future work.
works.difference: The prefetch starts at tool start (fixed trigger), not at predicted return minus fetch time minus queue. It is HBM only, with no SSD or host tier.
evidence_quotes: "Given an AEG, when node v completes inference and begins tool execution, we identify the most likely successor u= arg max u′ P(v→u′) and begin prefetching its prefix KV cache (if not already cached). Prefetching uses spare GPU memory and separate CUDA streams [50] to overlap with ongoing operations." (§4.3)
"We maintain per-tool-type latency distributions using exponential moving averages and set TTL to the p-th percentile of expected duration" (§4.2)
"FlexGen [55] explores host-DRAM offload extensively, and integrating it as a third eviction tier under WA-LRU prediction is straightforward future work." (§9.1.2)

works.title: PBKV: Efficient Serving for Dynamic Agent Workflows with Prediction-based KV-Cache Management
works.mechanism: Tiers: GPU radix tree plus SGLang HiCache host tier; no SSD. Signal: a GraphSAGE-based predictor of which agent is invoked in the next K steps. Start time: prefetch runs only on pure-decode batches, bounded by bandwidth × step duration, and only into idle GPU space.
works.difference: It predicts which agent comes next, not when a tool returns (tools are not modeled). It is host to GPU only. Its conservative prefetch, which never displaces valuable cache, addresses the harm of wasted prefetch, but not through timing.
evidence_quotes: "a two-tier KV-Cache storage organized as a Radix Tree on GPU memory and HiCache on host memory"

"PBKV therefore restricts prefetching to otherwise-idle GPU space and PCIe bandwidth, so that even under poor predictions, prefetching neither displaces valuable cache nor competes for on-path bandwidth."
"PBKV activates prefetching only on pure-decode batches (>90% of all batches in our measurements). Within such a batch, we bound the transferable volume as Sbw = Bandwidth·StepDuration"

works.title: CacheScout: Learning Agent Execution for KV-Cache Management in Agentic Serving (also 'A Policy-Driven Runtime Layer for Agentic LLM Serving', arXiv 2605.27744)
works.mechanism: vLLM with LMCache CPU offload. An online Markov chain over agents drives survival-based eviction. The 'prefetch' is a warmup request that recomputes the likely next agent's anchor (system prompt and tool definitions) between steps. It does not fetch from a lower tier and does not use tool-return timing.
works.difference: It precomputes a shared anchor rather than fetching the private session context from a lower tier, and it has no wall-clock timing. Its own ablation finds the prefetch alone is 'inert' on its workloads. Its related-work claim that [4,24,39] reload 'just before the tool returns' holds only for TokenCake [4]. No such mechanism was found in Autellix or Agent.xpu.
evidence_quotes: "the coordinator issues a lightweight warmup request containing only the predicted agent's reusable anchor, including its system prompt, tool definitions, and a minimal user prompt." (§3.4)
"On its own, prefetch is inert on these workloads: the median turn carries no warmable agent prefix"
"Another line of work fills the tool pause with other agents' work and reloads the paused agent's KV from CPU just before the tool returns [4, 24, 39]." (related work)

works.title: CachedAttention (AttentionStore): Cost-Efficient LLM Serving for Multi-turn Conversations
works.mechanism: Tiers: GPU, host DRAM and disk. Scheduler-aware fetching prefetches disk to host for jobs already in the job queue, with a look-ahead window of Cmem/Skv. Scheduler-aware eviction avoids evicting KV of jobs in a look-ahead eviction window. Session KV has a TTL.
works.difference: It has the SSD-to-host prefetch, but the trigger is queue entry, i.e., after the request arrives. This is the baseline T1 wants to beat. The prefetch window is bounded by host capacity and eviction is aware of queued jobs, which touches the T2 concern. There is no prediction of the next turn's arrival.
evidence_quotes: "If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed. The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory." (§3.3.1)
"the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv."

works.title: Strata: Hierarchical Context Caching for Long Context Language Model Serving
works.mechanism: Storage-to-host prefetch starts when a storage hit is detected for a request, overlaps with that request's queuing delay, and is terminated when the request is dispatched. This matches the queue-entry trigger in the user's HiCache build (scheduler.py:3148-3155: _add_request_to_queue calls self._prefetch_kvcache(req), then waiting_queue.append(req)).
works.difference: This is the design T1 critiques: the fetch is hidden only by the queue wait, so a shallow queue exposes it. There is no prediction before arrival.
evidence_quotes: "the cache controller opportunistically prefetches data from storage to host memory when a cache hit is detected at the storage layer. The latency of this prefetch overlaps the request's queuing delay. Once the scheduler dispatches the request for execution, the cache controller terminates any in-flight prefetch and leverages the available cache already in host or GPU memory." (§4.2.1)

works.title: LMCache: An Efficient KV Cache Layer for Enterprise-Scale LLM Inference
works.mechanism: Asynchronous prefetch of queued queries' KV from slower tiers (remote disk) to CPU or GPU while the query waits in the queue. The target tier is configurable.
works.difference: The trigger is queue-based, after arrival, with no tool or turn prediction.
evidence_quotes: "if a query (with cache hit) arrives when the inference engine is processing other queries, the arriving query has to wait in queue. LMCACHE exploits this idle interval to prefetch the queued queries' KV cache from slower storage tiers into faster ones (e.g., from remote disk to local CPU memory or GPU memory)." (§5)

works.title: PCR: A Prefetch-Enhanced Cache Reuse System for Low-Latency RAG Serving
works.mechanism: Queue-based SSD-to-DRAM prefetch for requests still in the waiting queue, plus look-ahead LRU that protects chunks needed by queued requests.
works.difference: The trigger comes after arrival, and the workload is RAG with no agent or tool gap. Look-ahead eviction is T2-adjacent.
evidence_quotes: "a queue-based prefetching mechanism that prefetches the KV caches from SSD to DRAM when requests are still in waiting queue"
"a look-ahead LRU replacement policy that uses pending requests in the scheduler queue"

works.title: Where Should the KV Cache Live? Placement Policies Across GPU, CPU, and SSD for Long-Lived Sessions
works.mechanism: A discrete-event simulator over HBM, DRAM and SSD comparing recency, reuse-frequency, predicted-reuse and EWMA next-touch policies, with a swept prefetch lookahead that moves blocks the resuming session will need, across chat, agent and document-QA workloads.
works.difference: It is a simulation with block-level lookahead, not timed by tool return. It is a negative result: speculative fetches on a contended link delay demand fetches. This is a risk for T1 given the user's 1.88 GiB/s SSD.
evidence_quotes: "Prefetching does not justify its bandwidth cost. Across the policy and cache size grid, even an oracle with knowledge of future requests never beats no prefetch on migration traffic." (abstract)
"on a contended link a speculative fetch delays the demand fetch a request is waiting on, and that cost exceeds the stall it removes whenever the workload's reuse is not tightly predictable."

works.title: MORI: Idleness is Relative: Exploiting Tool-Call Idle Windows for Offloading in Agentic Systems
works.mechanism: Tiers: GPU HBM and CPU DRAM. Programs are ranked by continuous idleness; the busiest stay on GPU and the most idle go to CPU. Promotion to GPU prefers CPU-queue programs that have already completed their tool call. It deliberately avoids per-call duration prediction.
works.difference: Reload is reactive, after completion, and 2-tier. It notes that chat-era offloading assumes gaps long enough to 'reload it before the next', but it does not time reloads by a predicted return.
evidence_quotes: "Promotion to GPU. When GPU capacity becomes available, the scheduler promotes programs in a priority order: (1) CPU-queue programs that have completed their tool call and are waiting for inference"

"These methods mainly target the chatbot use case, where inter-turn gaps are dominated by human typing latency (typically tens of seconds), leaving ample time to offload KV cache after each turn and reload it before the next."

works.title: CacheWise: Understanding Workloads and Optimizing KVCache Management for Efficiently Serving LLM Coding Agents
works.mechanism: Reuse-aware eviction guided by predicted next-use time from tool-call metadata (names and arguments). In its offload configuration, blocks go to CPU DRAM and are 'swapped back on demand when the corresponding session resumes'.
works.difference: The predicted next use drives eviction only. Swap-in is on demand, and there is no SSD prefetch.
evidence_quotes: "evicted blocks are transferred from GPU memory to CPU DRAM and swapped back on demand when the corresponding session resumes"
"CacheWise combines prefix-aware scheduling with reuse-aware eviction guided by lightweight predictions from tool call metadata." (abstract)

works.title: vLLM x AgentX: Optimizing for Real-World Agentic Serving (vLLM blog) and vLLM router issue #285 (Program-level Progress-TTL)
works.mechanism: The blog lists prefetch during inter-turn gaps as planned future work; hierarchical CPU and disk tiers exist via Mooncake Store. The router RFC protects KV logically with a TTL computed from empirical tool-return intervals and lists DRAM/SSD prefetch as a non-goal.
works.difference: Stated as future work or a non-goal only. No mechanism or timing rule.
evidence_quotes: Blog: "Inter-turn gaps create an opportunity to move the retained KV state toward the worker likely to serve the next turn. Prefetching during this idle interval can hide transfer latency and reduce cold resumptions." (section 'The path ahead: planned optimizations and future work')
Router #285 non-goal: "Introducing DRAM/SSD offloading or prefetch control in the initial implementation"

works.title: ThunderAgent: A Simple, Fast and Program-Aware Agentic Inference System
works.mechanism: Program-aware scheduling and migration. It characterizes existing tiered systems (Pensieve, Continuum, Strata, ShadowKV) as prefetching back to GPU upon resumption, and argues that swap cycles negate the benefit in high-frequency agent workflows.
works.difference: It confirms that prior tiered systems restore on resumption, i.e., reactively. It also counter-argues that tier round-trips can cost more than they save.
evidence_quotes: "These tiered caching mechanisms mitigate transient preemption by offloading inactive KV states to lower-tier storage and prefetching them back to GPU upon request resumption."
"In high-frequency agentic workflows, the overhead of frequent swap-in and swap-out cycles often negates the benefits of multi-tier caching as shown in Section 5."

works.title: KVCache Cache in the Wild: Characterizing and Optimizing KVCache Cache at a Large Cloud Provider
works.mechanism: A trace study showing that KV reuse time is predictable per request category (roughly exponential). The prediction is used for a workload-aware eviction policy, not for prefetch.
works.difference: It supports T1's premise that the gap is predictable, using production data, but only for eviction.
evidence_quotes: "for each specific request category (type plus turn number), the reuse time is predictable based on the historical information (§3.4)."
"we further propose a workload-aware cache eviction policy that improves the serving performance"

works.title: Adaptive KV Retention for LLM Agents at Human-Approval Timescales
works.mechanism: Retention across HBM, host DRAM or discard for minute-to-hour human-approval pauses, priced by GPU opportunity cost. A host-resident copy pays its restore cost at resume. Retention is load-indexed, without per-request wait prediction.
works.difference: Restore happens at resume, with no pre-arrival fetch. This is the closest 'human think time' work found; it does not prefetch.
evidence_quotes: "A host-resident copy pays restore cost β2 at resume, while discarded state pays recomputation cost β3."
"the controller selects between indefinite retention and load-indexed expiration using calibration wait samples, without requiring per-request wait prediction." (abstract)

works.title: Predictive Multi-Tier Memory Management for KV Cache in Large-Scale GPU Inference
works.venue_year: arXiv 2604.26968 (single author; v2 Aug 2026; component validation plus analytical projections)
works.mechanism: A six-tier hierarchy. A Markov chain over tool invocations fires when a tool switch is detected by output parsing and 'initiates prefetching of tool-context blocks from lower tiers'.
works.difference: The trigger is tool-switch detection, not predicted return time, and there is no queue term. End-to-end gains are analytical projections, not measurements.
evidence_quotes: "When a tool switch is detected (via output parsing), the system: (1) pre-allocates KV cache capacity for the predicted next tool; (2) adjusts head-granular importance multipliers based on the transition type; (3) initiates prefetching of tool-context blocks from lower tiers."

result.novelty_assessment:
Verdict: Takeaway 1 is not novel as stated. Its core idea is already published: restore a session's KV during the tool gap, timed by a predicted tool return, so the transfer is off the critical path. The published versions are GPU/DRAM only, and none uses an SSD tier or an expected queue wait. So T1 is defensible as a narrower, incremental system design, but not as a new idea.

Refutation (prior art a reviewer will cite):
(1) TokenCake (arXiv 2510.18586; EuroSys '27 per its README).
 - It offloads idle KV to CPU during function calls.
 - "As the predicted completion time approaches, the scheduler begins a gradual upload ... to hide transfer latency".
 - The prediction comes from a per-function-type EWMA blended with a user estimate.
(2) Ask the Tool (arXiv 2609.18849, 16 Sep 2026).
 - With a DRAM tier, it "refreshes the context one lead time before the predicted return and reloads it if it has gone".
 - The lead time is the time needed to get the context back.
(3) Work that starts a fetch before arrival without a return-time model:
 - KVFlow (NeurIPS 2025, built on SGLang) prefetches CPU to GPU while the previous agent runs.
 - SAGA (2026) starts prefetching the likely successor's KV when the tool starts.
(4) SGLang RFC #27574 (June 2026) proposes this for HiCache, including L3.
 - "Prefetch: Move KV into a hotter tier before it is needed"; "the KV offloaded during a pause is the KV warmed back before the continuation resumes".
 - It explicitly defers it: "TODO - measure request-time L3 restoration before adding proactive Prefetch".
 - The vLLM AgentX blog (2026-09-08) lists inter-turn prefetch as future work.
(5) Of CacheScout's three citations for reloading "just before the tool returns", only TokenCake holds up. Autellix and Agent.xpu do not do this; I checked their text.

What survives (not found in any examined source):
(a) An SSD-to-host stage of the pre-arrival restore.
 - Every published pre-return restore is 2-tier: TokenCake's GPU/CPU with a 100 GB CPU pool, and Ask the Tool's HBM+DRAM.
 - SSD-to-host prefetch exists only with a queue-entry trigger: CachedAttention (ATC'24), LMCache, Strata and PCR.
 - That trigger is exactly the HiCache behavior the user measured: scheduler.py:3148-3155, where _add_request_to_queue calls self._prefetch_kvcache(req) and then self.waiting_queue.append(req).
 - The lead times differ by orders of magnitude. TokenCake uploads 256 blocks (4K tokens) in 31.7 ms. The user's x70 SSD restores ran at 2.6–3.3 s p50, which is where prediction error and bandwidth contention matter.
(b) A start time that includes an estimated queueing delay (start ≈ predicted return + E[queue wait] − fetch time).
 - TokenCake's window is T_FC − T_transfer.
 - Ask the Tool's budget is only the recovery time.
 - Continuum estimates queueing delay but uses it for the GPU retention TTL, not for prefetch timing.
(c) Adapting the timing to load: earlier when the queue is shallow, later or never when it is deep. Paired with Takeaway 2, no published policy does this.
(d) Placement of the gap signal: the user wants it emitted from the end of a request inside SGLang HiCache. The SGLang RFCs carry only hints (expected_tool_duration_ms, kv.prefetch for the current request), with no timing policy.

Evidence against the proposed mechanism (must be addressed, or the reviewer wins):
 - T1's proposed signal is "an estimated tool return time distribution", which is history-based. Ask the Tool reports that the best history predictor triggers in time in 0%, 0% and 13% of test, build and script runs, versus 31%, 15% and 50% for live progress. It also reports that history predictors fetch back 8–13x more volume than needed.
 - TokenCake itself regresses 8.3% at noise 0.25 ("mistimed uploads").
 - A GPU/CPU/SSD simulation (arXiv 2609.16215) found that even oracle prefetch never beats no-prefetch on migration traffic, because speculative fetches delay demand fetches on a contended link. The user's SSD read path is 1.88 GiB/s, so this applies.
 - ThunderAgent argues that swap cycles negate the benefit of tiering in high-frequency agent workloads.
 - TokenCake's released code still does only demand-triggered recovery.

Is it a legitimate, motivatable design? Yes, as a scoped claim: "3-tier, queue-aware, just-in-time SSD-to-host restore for agent sessions".
 - Motivation from the user's data: at x70, overall TTFT is 0.3 s p50, but about 20% of returns are restored from SSD at 2.6–3.3 s p50, and their queue wait is mostly the L3 read.
 - Required framing: position it as extending TokenCake and Ask the Tool to the SSD tier with a queue-delay term, and cite the SGLang RFC as unimplemented intent.
 - Required reporting: separate oracle gaps (the replay's trace gap × scale is deterministic) from realistic predictors, including a quantile-based start and a progress-signal variant.
 - Required measurements: the extra host occupancy and host evictions caused by early fetches, which is where T2 interacts; x70 host evictions began at about 1.56M live tokens.
 - At x10/x1 (queue waits around 100 s), the queue already hides the fetch, so T1's benefit should be claimed only for sparse regimes.

t1.verdict: Partially supported. Worth building for the sparse regime (x70) only, once the mechanism is corrected. The idea itself is not new. The SSD restore really is exposed: 19-20% of x70 returning turns are restored from SSD, at 2.8-3.3 s p50 TTFT against 0.25 s for host hits. The next turn is near-certain (97%), and gaps of at least 47 s leave plenty of lead time, so in simulation a pre-arrival fetch hides 81-100% of the read. But most of the exposed time is queueing behind other SSD reads, which are issued reactively, served one at a time and arrive in bursts. It is not mainly a shallow queue failing to hide a single read. The lead has to cover the L3 backlog (about 10-20 s here), and it must stay below L2 survival time (roughly 20-30 s at peak) unless the fetched pages are protected. The replays cannot show that gaps are predictable: history-based predictors keep only 54-71% of the benefit, and an over-estimate of 25% or more keeps none.
what_is_right: Tier resolution is tied to arrival. _add_request_to_queue calls self._prefetch_kvcache(req) and then waiting_queue.append(req) (scheduler.py:3148-3155). prefetch_start matches ReqTimeStats entry_time within 1-2 ms (n=4,659/4,660, x1 SSD arms).

The SSD fetch is on the critical path. wait_complete skips the request until its fetch ends (scheduler.py:3817-3821). L3 insert to admission is p50 0.00 s at x70. Storage-hit TTFT p50 is 2.76 s (to) / 3.34 s (wc), against 0.25 / 0.24 s for host hits.

The private context is reused. 4,548 of 4,676 replies (97.3%) are followed by another turn. Storage hits restore about 20.3-20.5K tokens of prompts around 29K, so fetching a session's last context is wasted only on final turns (about 3%).
There is lead time. Every x70 L3-hit gap is at least 46.9 s (to) / 47.9 s (wc), p50 52 / 84 s. A turn's own read takes about 0.8-0.9 s, and even congested fetch windows stay at or below 20-22 s.

Starting before arrival works when timed against the true arrival. In a single-reader EDF simulation (validated, median io_end error -0.029 s), a 10 s lead hides 81-91% of fetch time and a 20 s lead about 100%. Storage-hit TTFT mean falls 5.18 -> 1.27 s (to) and 5.57 -> 0.32 s (wc).
The SSD has spare bandwidth to shift reads into. The read thread is busy 23-27% of the read span (73-77% idle), but 85-89% during the +1200-1500 s burst.
what_is_wrong_or_imprecise: Mechanism. A shallow queue is not the main cause. Storage hits that arrive to an empty queue (37-39% of hits) expose only about 0.7 s each and carry 5-7% of fetch-window time. Hits arriving at queue depth >=5 carry 72-81% of it, and that queue is mostly other requests waiting for L3: corr(queue depth, pending reads) = 0.85 / 0.99. Waiting on the single L3 read thread (cache_controller.py:447-448, 1136-1141) is 58% (to) / 80% (wc) of storage-hit TTFT. In bursts, 10-s offered read demand reaches about 2.1x the SSD bandwidth.

The queue-entry 'prefetch' is only an L3->L2 fetch. It covers only the suffix that L1+L2 miss, and only if that suffix is at least 256 tokens (unified_radix_cache.py:1759-1769). The L2->L1 load happens at admission (schedule_policy.py:1305-1316).

Timing. 'Estimated tool return minus fetch time' gives too short a lead. Moving each fetch earlier by only its own read time (size / bandwidth) hides just 16-24%, because early restores still collide with each other. The lead must include the predicted L3 backlog (10-20 s here), and reads must be served in order of predicted deadline (EDF), not FIFO.

'Even earlier' has an upper limit. Fetched pages are inserted unlocked (unified_radix_cache.py:2024). Fetching at the end of the reply re-evicts 77% of fetched contexts (net 13-19% of fetch time hidden) and parks an average of 37% of L2. Without protection, leads of 30 s / 60 s re-evict 20-25% / 56-64%.

Gap predictability is assumed, not shown. The replay gaps are deterministic trace gaps x70, and 37% of them fall in 49-53 s. History predictors land within ±25% for only 34-50% of L3-hit turns, and they are biased low, because the turns that fall to L3 are the ones with long gaps. Any over-estimate of 25% or more loses the whole benefit. Tool-call-based prediction is not tested by this data. Ask the Tool reports about 80% median error for history predictors.

The queueing-delay estimate must be server-side. The replay client's default aiohttp 100-connection cap (replay_agentic.py:265) adds lag that the server never sees: p50 0.07 s at x70, but 2-7 s at x10/x1 (p95 42-51 s).
Scope. This applies to the sparse regime only. At x10/x1, storage hits are 0.1-0.2% of turns, and queue waits of about 100 s would hide any read.

Part of the SSD residency that T1 targets comes from inclusion. About 40% of L2 mirrors L1. A session-level LRU model predicts that reclaiming that mirror would cut x70 SSD/cold returns from 21% to 2.7-4.5%, which would shrink T1's opportunity.
t1.corrected_statement: In the sparse regime (x70), about one returning turn in five (19.7% / 18.6%) finds its private context only on SSD. HiCache resolves tiers only when the request reaches the scheduler, so each SSD restore starts at arrival, and a single read thread serves restores in FIFO order. Restores arrive in bursts: 10-s offered demand reaches about 2.1x the 1.88 GiB/s SSD, even though the SSD is about 75% idle overall. A typical restore therefore waits 3.0-4.4 s behind other restores, plus about 0.85 s for its own read. Storage-hit TTFT is 2.8-3.3 s p50 (5.2-5.6 s mean), against 0.25 s for host hits. A session's next turn is near-certain (97%) and follows a gap of at least about 47 s, so the restore can start before the turn arrives, under three conditions. (a) Reads are served earliest predicted arrival first. (b) The lead covers the read plus the predicted L3 backlog: about 10-20 s here, not the roughly 1 s read time. (c) The fetched pages are protected in L2 until used, or the lead is kept short enough to survive L2 turnover; without protection, leads beyond about 30 s are mostly re-evicted. Timed against the true arrivals, this hides 81-100% of the fetch and cuts mean returning TTFT by 40-66%. With realistic gap predictors it keeps roughly 54-88% of that gain. An over-estimate of 25% or more falls back to today's behaviour. These replays do not test whether the tool-call type predicts return time well enough.

Their net is 54-71%, plus 500-700 GiB of extra SSD reads against 1,810 / 1,571 GiB actually read (t1_pred.py, t1_net.py).

The queue-entry SSD->host prefetch that T1 criticizes (the baseline): CachedAttention (ATC'24), Strata (arXiv 2508.18572), LMCache (arXiv 2510.09665), SGLang HiCache.

Alternative remedy and counter-evidence. Cake (arXiv 2410.03065) overlaps load with compute instead of starting the load earlier. arXiv 2609.16215 finds speculative prefetch does not pay on a contended link, even with an oracle.

t2.verdict: Partially supported. The symptom is real and is the largest prize in the data. At x10/x1, 93-95% of all prefill recomputes context that was in L1+L2 when the request arrived and on SSD the whole time. That clearly motivates a redesign, but the stated mechanism is mostly wrong. The dominant loss involves no prefetch: the context matched in L1/L2 at arrival is evicted while the request waits. Three things combine. (1) LRU plus the refresh at arrival makes eviction follow FCFS order, so the queue head goes first. (2) The pressure comes from write-through of other requests' prefill completions, which are mostly recomputes themselves (a self-reinforcing loop). (3) Admission re-checks only L1/L2, so the context is never re-fetched. Prefetched pages evicted before use are only 0.4-1.9% of lost tokens. Writes happen mainly at end of prefill, not at request end. The host/HBM 'lock' coupling is structural inclusion: about 40% of L2 mirrors L1. 'Start the prefetch later' has to become: re-resolve against L3 before admission, protect the result until admission, and evict in order of predicted admission. The core idea is published (CachedAttention, ATC'24), and a reactive admission-time re-query is already merged upstream (SGLang #39283/#40042).
what_is_right: Write-through is eager and complete. write_through_threshold = 1 (unified_radix_cache.py:465-467). Every host-written page is also written to SSD 1:1: d2h tokens = h2s tokens in all 6 SSD runs, with 0 L3 cleanups. So every context later lost from L2 was still on SSD (inferred from the aggregates; not checked per rid).
Content found or fetched long before processing gets lost before use. At x1 the loss rate is 0% for server waits under 10 s, 29-35% at 20-30 s, and >=94% beyond 60 s. The median server wait is 111 s.

The literal case does occur in the class that ran. Prefetched pages are inserted and unlocked as soon as the read completes (unified_radix_cache.py:2562-2566, 1983, 2024). At x10/x1, 80-87% of real L3 reads were evicted again before admission (58/68, 57/66, 12/15, 13/15), and each lost its whole span.
Host eviction is forced by other requests' write-through. At x10, 6,667 of 6,723 evict_host events (52.3M of 53.4M tokens) sit next to a d2h_submit; prefetch staging accounts for only 1.08M tokens.
Recomputation follows. 49-55% of returning turns are admitted with only the 7,808-token shared prompt, and these recomputes are 93-95% of all prefill.
Moving the fetch toward processing time is feasible. Re-reading each admitted context just in time needs about 0.6-0.7 GiB/s (32-37% of the SSD) at x1's admission rate.

The host/HBM coupling is a real capacity loss. About 40% of L2 (636-656K tokens) holds copies of device-resident KV in every run, and host eviction began exactly when cumulative write-through reached the size of L2.
what_is_wrong_or_imprecise: Write timing: it is not 'right after the request is done'. 72-98% of host and SSD write volume is written when the last prefill chunk completes (cache_unfinished_req with chunked=False, batch_result_processor.py:353-359), before the first token. Only the decode pages and the page straddling the prompt boundary are written at finish. Intermediate chunks are never backed up (chunked=True). Each SSD write is chained to its host-write ack, with p50 lag 0.02 s at x70 and 0.28-0.34 s at x10/x1.

The dominant loss is not a prefetch. At arrival the history is almost always still in L1+L2 (98.4-99.6% of returns), so no L3 fetch is issued: an L3 query hits >=256 tokens for only 68/4,538 (x10) and 15/4,548 (x1) returns. Prefetched-then-evicted content is 0.4-1.9% of lost tokens; 98-99.6% of lost tokens belong to turns with no L3 load.

Missing cause 1: nothing protects the match while the request waits. The only protection is the prefetch anchor host lock. It is never taken when the unmatched tail is under 256 tokens. It is dropped within milliseconds when L3 holds fewer than 256 matching tokens (prefetch_start->s2h_query p50 1 ms). After a successful fetch it is dropped at insert.

Missing cause 2: the eviction order is the worst possible one. The arrival-time match refreshes last_access_time (unified_tree_core.py:836-839), and host eviction pops the oldest node (evict_policy.py:17-18). So eviction follows FCFS order, and the queue head, which is admitted next, goes first. The queued working set (0.9-1.8M private tokens) is larger than the host-only part of L2 (at most 0.96M).

Missing cause 3: nothing re-checks L3 at admission. Admission re-matches only L1/L2; check_prefetch_progress returns True when there is no ongoing prefetch. The paced retry is off (poll interval 0). Even when enabled, it counts scheduling passes and allows at most 4 attempts, so it is not tied to admission (memory.py:169-183, scheduler.py:3118-3146). Upstream's admission-time re-query is absent from this fork (grep count 0). As a result the SSD tier adds nothing: 54-60% of admissions have only the shared prompt at x10/x1, with or without SSD.

'Newly finished requests' should read 'other requests' prefill completions'. These are 98% of write volume at x10/x1, and most are recomputed prompts. x10/x1 write 54-58M tokens against 5.3M at x70, which is the self-reinforcing loop.

'Lock status' is the wrong mechanism. lock_ref and host_lock_ref are separate counters. What pins host copies is _is_host_leaf (unified_tree_core.py:1889): it rejects any node whose device copy still exists, locked or idle, so under write_through L2 always contains L1. Duplicates are reclaimed only under write_back (unified_tree_core.py:1497), which pays a synchronous D2H on eviction, about 50x the per-token cost of a demote.

The mirror is about 40% of L2 in every regime. The part that is idle and cheap to reclaim is 28.7-30.6% of L2 in the x70 SSD arms, but only 3-6.7% at x10/x1. One data agent estimated 15-18% for x70 hbm_host, but that model assumed running requests' prompts are not backed up, which the prefill-end write evidence contradicts.

The remedy is incomplete. 'Start the prefetch later' cannot help the dominant case, because there is no prefetch to delay. It needs three things: re-resolve against L3 near admission, protect what is found or fetched until admission, and evict in order of predicted admission. Pinning every queued prefix is infeasible (about 1.59M tokens, roughly all of L2).
The queue-delay input must be server-side. 19.9 s of the 131.2 s mean x1 TTFT is client-side lag from the connection cap, which the server never sees.
t2.corrected_statement: Under dense load (x10/x1), write-through backs up each new prompt to host when its prefill completes (72-98% of all write volume) and the decode tail at finish. Every page is then chained to SSD, so the SSD holds every context. A returning turn nearly always still finds its whole previous context in L1+L2 when it reaches the server (98.4-99.6%). So no SSD prefetch is issued, and nothing protects that match while the request waits (median 111 s at x1). Host eviction, forced by other requests' write-through (mostly recomputed prompts), removes the oldest host leaves first. Because the arrival-time match refreshed their LRU stamps, eviction follows FCFS order, and the queue head, next to be admitted, goes first. Admission re-matches only L1/L2 and never asks the SSD again. As a result, 49-55% of returning turns recompute everything except the 7,808-token shared prompt. That is 93-95% of all prefill, and it feeds more write-through and longer queues, a self-reinforcing loop. Prefetched content evicted before admission is a minor special case (0.4-1.9% of lost tokens). The fix is to resolve tiers relative to admission, not arrival: re-resolve against the SSD shortly before predicted admission (from queue position and admission rate), protect what is found or fetched until admission, and evict in order of predicted admission (queue tail first). Pinning the whole queue is infeasible (about 1.59M tokens, all of L2). Separately, the host/HBM coupling is inclusion, not locking. A host copy can be evicted only after its device copy is gone, so about 40% of L2 mirrors L1 in every run. That is a capacity lever independent of timing.

Predicted vs logged d2h agree within 0.03% in all 9 runs. On isolated x70 turns, 24,640 tokens were written at prefill end (= expected), 16,064 at finish, 0 during decode (split.py, wt_timing.py).

SSD holds everything: d2h tokens = h2s tokens exactly (53,918,976 x10 to; 57,967,168 x1 to; all 6 SSD runs). 0 'NIXL L3 cleanup' lines and 0 evict_host with tokens<requested. h2s lag p50 0.02 s (x70), 0.28-0.34 s (x10/x1).

Present at arrival: the whole previous context was in L1+L2 for 98.4% (x10) / 99.6% (x1) of returns. Arrival match / prompt p50 0.99 vs admitted cached / prompt p50 0.35-0.37. Median arrival match 23.2-23.4K tokens vs cached at admission 7,808. Arrival match = P - 1 - prefetch_start.tokens.

Not a prefetch: 98.1% (x10 to) and 99.6% (x1 to) of lost tokens are in turns with no L3 load. The literal case: real L3 reads lost 58/68 and 57/66 (x10), 12/15 and 13/15 (x1), i.e. 0.91-0.94M and 0.21M tokens, or 0.4-1.9% of lost tokens.

Unprotected: tail <256 tokens means no lock (1,167 lost turns at x10 to, 1,309 at x1 to). An L3 miss releases the lock at the next drain, with prefetch_start->s2h_query p50 1 ms, p99 3-10 ms (1,252 / 1,408 lost turns). Fetched pages are unlocked at insert (unified_radix_cache.py:2024).

closest_prior_work: CachedAttention/AttentionStore (USENIX ATC'24). Fetches from disk to host only for a look-ahead window of Lpw = Cmem/Skv queued jobs, and exempts jobs in a longer look-ahead eviction window from eviction, evicting from the tail first. This is T2's core idea, but counted in jobs rather than time, with whole-session items, no in-gap sessions and no write-through interaction.

SGLang upstream #39283/#40042 (merged Sep 2026). _prefetch_after_device_hit_loss re-issues the L3 lookup at admission when the device+host match has shrunk since arrival, and skips the request meanwhile. It is reactive: the fetch latency stays on the critical path. #40011 names 'the device match evicts while the request is queued'. #31887 (unmerged) proposes waiting-queue retries, admission deadlines and an isolated staging partition. #32724 notes that staging finalisation is tied to the FCFS scan.

py-kvcache (arXiv 2609.11744) with vLLM #49902/#50014. Disk->CPU promotions for queued requests are evicted before use and the request recomputes. The remedy is a bounded lookahead plus protection of promotions not yet read.
PCR (arXiv 2603.23049). SSD->DRAM prefetch for a fixed 4-request window of the waiting queue, plus a look-ahead LRU that protects chunks pending requests need.
LMCache vLLM adapter and vLLM v1 connector. The external lookup happens only at the admission scan (the 'late' extreme), and looked-up KV is pinned until the request is scheduled.

Continuum (arXiv 2511.02230) uses a tool-duration CDF plus queueing delay, the same inputs T1/T2 propose, but for a GPU retention TTL, not fetch timing. Adaptive KV Retention (arXiv 2608.30830) sets load-indexed host residency via Little's law.

Classic theory: Cao et al., SIGMETRICS'95 (Do No Harm; a prefetch reserves its slot early). Patterson et al., TIP, SOSP'95 (prefetch horizon). Kimbrel et al., OSDI'96 (fixed horizon / forestall: one just-in-time rule that turns aggressive under backlog).
For the inclusion sub-point: SGLang's own write_back policy (_reclaim_full_host_duplicates, unified_tree_core.py:1497-1556) is the existing non-inclusive design.

result.unified_design:
Admission-anchored staging (AAS). Every tier decision for a session's next turn is driven by one quantity: its predicted admission time Â, the time the scheduler will actually start its prefill. Today these decisions are driven by the request's arrival time.

1. State
- A session registry, keyed by session id, holds for each live session s:
  - a handle to the radix path committed by its last turn (last node or page-hash chain, n_s tokens, and which pages are in L1, L2 or L3);
  - its status: in-gap, queued or running;
  - Â_s.
- The registry is filled at cache_finished_req (turn end, time t_e). It is updated on arrival and on every scheduling pass.

2. Predicting Â
- In-gap session: Â_s = t_e + Ĝ_q + Ŵ.
  - Ĝ_q is a low quantile (q ≈ 0.1-0.25) of the return-time distribution for this tool type, or a harness hint or live progress when one is available.
  - Ŵ is the predicted server-side wait: requests ahead / μ̂, where μ̂ is the EWMA admission rate.
- Queued at FCFS position p: Â_s = now + p/μ̂, refined by the expected completions of the running batch.
- While a tool is overdue, Â is re-estimated from the residual gap distribution. On arrival, Ĝ is replaced by the true arrival time.
- Only the server-side wait counts. The client's 100-connection cap must be removed first.

3. Timing rule
- Issue the L3→L2 read for s's pages that are not in L1/L2 at S_s = Â_s − (n_s^L3 · 98,304 B / BW + Backlog_EDF(Â_s)/BW + m).
  - BW is the measured SSD read bandwidth.
  - Backlog_EDF is the bytes of pending reads with an earlier Â.
  - m ≈ 2 s is a safety margin.
- The read never starts earlier than Â_s − H, where H is the park horizon.
- Reads are served earliest-Â first (EDF), not FIFO. They run as low-priority traffic that yields to demand reads, and reads plus write-through are paced to stay under BW.
- The same rule covers both regimes with no mode switch:
  - Sparse (Ŵ ≈ 0): the read starts before arrival, with a lead of about 10-20 s at x70 (Takeaway 1).
  - Dense (Ŵ ≫ H): the read starts after arrival, once the request is within p ≤ μ̂ · (read + backlog + m) ≈ 1-2 positions of the head at x1 (Takeaway 2).

4. Residency and protection rule
- For every s with Â_s − now ≤ H, protect both its arrival-time L1/L2 match and any pages staged for it.
  - Protection runs from the moment they are matched or land until admission, when the device lock takes over.
  - Today this match is unprotected when the tail is under 256 tokens, protected for only milliseconds after an L3 miss, and unprotected after insert.
- Use a soft host priority class, not host_lock_ref. Hard locks can make write-through backups skip (unified_radix_cache.py:1412-1414).
- Budget: the sum of n_s over protected sessions must be ≤ β · (L2 − L1 mirror − write-through reserve). If it is over, shrink H so only the earliest-Â sessions stay protected. This is a CachedAttention-style window measured in seconds.
- Little's law sizes it at about μ̂ · H · n̄:
  - x1: 0.362/s × 10 s × 20.6K ≈ 75K tokens ≈ 5% of L2.
  - x70 with a 10-20 s lead: 5-14% of L2 on average, 27% at peak.

5. Eviction order
- Among unprotected host leaves, evict the latest predicted admission first: the queue tail and sessions with long predicted gaps.
- Use LRU only for content that has no session prediction.
- This replaces the arrival-time LRU refresh, which today makes eviction order equal FCFS order and evicts the queue head first.
- Do No Harm: staging for s may only evict content whose Â is later than Â_s.

6. Fallback at admission
- When the FCFS scan reaches s, re-match L1/L2.
- If the match is shorter than the registry expects, re-query L3 with the semantics of upstream _prefetch_after_device_hit_loss.
  - Skip s while the read runs, under a deadline.
  - Choose load or recompute by cost: backlog + read time vs prefill time at current throughput.
- If s arrives before S_s (the gap was over-predicted), start the fetch at arrival. The worst case is therefore today's behaviour.
- If Â slips beyond H, drop protection and re-arm the fetch if the pages are later evicted. A final turn (2.7% of replies) releases immediately.

7. Feedback
- Per regime, measure lateness (fetch finished after admission) and pollution (staged or protected bytes evicted or unused).
- Adapt q, m, H and β from these, as in feedback-directed prefetching (FDP).

8. Optional capacity lever (ablated separately)
- Under host pressure, reclaim the L2 mirrors of idle device-resident nodes whose SSD write has been acked.
- When such a node is later evicted from the device, demote it straight to L3-only, since the SSD already holds every page. If Â is near, re-copy it asynchronously instead.
- This gives non-inclusive L1/L2 without write_back's synchronous D2H.

Signals it needs
- Session id.
- Turn-end event with tool-call type and arguments, plus an optional declared-duration hint or live progress.
- Per-tool gap quantiles, learned online.
- FCFS queue position, EWMA admission rate, and completion estimates for the running batch.
- L3 read backlog in bytes, and measured SSD read and write bandwidth.
- L2 occupancy, mirror size, host eviction rate and protected-budget use.
- A per-session residency map (which pages are in L1, L2, L3).

Hooks in the fork
- Registry: at cache_finished_req.
- Controller: polled from check_hicache_events (scheduler.py:3686).
- Protection: keep fetched pages protected past insert (unified_radix_cache.py:2024), and cover sub-256 tails and L3 misses (1759-1769, 2533).
- Eviction key: evict_policy.py:17-18 and full_component.py:243-253.
- EDF reads: in the prefetch IO thread (cache_controller.py:1136-1141).
- Admission re-check: beside check_prefetch_progress (scheduler.py:3817-3821).
result.novelty_position:
Neither takeaway is new as an idea, and a paper should claim neither.

Takeaway 1 (early restore): already published or announced.
- Restoring before the turn arrives, timed by a predicted tool return, is published for DRAM→HBM:
  - TokenCake (EuroSys '27);
  - Ask the Tool (arXiv 2609.18849);
  - SYMPHONY's expected_arrival advisories;
  - KVFlow, SAGA and PBKV, which key on workflow steps rather than time.
- For storage it is announced but not built: NVIDIA Dynamo's prefetch hooks, SGLang RFC #27574 (Prefetch is a TODO), and the vLLM and llm-d roadmaps.

Takeaway 2 (late restore and protection): already published, and partly merged upstream.
- Disk→host prefetch bound to queue position, plus eviction exemption for queued work, is CachedAttention (ATC '24). PCR and py-kvcache / vLLM #50014 are recent variants.
- SGLang upstream has merged a reactive admission-time L3 re-query (#39283/#40042). PR #40011 already names queue-time eviction.

The combined rule and its inputs: also prior art.
- A single just-in-time rule that fetches aggressively under backlog and late otherwise is Kimbrel et al.'s forestall (OSDI '96). TIP's prefetch horizon and Cao et al.'s Do-No-Harm give the theory.
- Continuum already combines a tool-duration CDF with a queueing-delay estimate, but uses them for GPU retention, not fetch timing.

What is defensible:
1. The measurement. On real SWE-agent traces, in a three-tier radix-tree engine, deciding tiers at arrival fails in both regimes, by different mechanisms.
   - Sparse regime: SSD reads are issued reactively, run one at a time on a single thread, and arrive in bursts. 58-80% of storage-hit TTFT is spent waiting behind other restores, while the SSD is about 75% idle.
   - Dense regime: the context matched at arrival is left unprotected. LRU plus FCFS evicts the head of the queue first, under write-through pressure that is itself mostly recompute. As a result 93-95% of prefill recomputes context that is still on the SSD, and the SSD tier contributes nothing.
   - In both regimes, inclusive mirroring costs about 40% of L2.
   - The same x70 load shows 59.5 s mean TTFT without SSD and 1.5-1.9 s with it, which suggests the regime is partly created by the cache policy itself.
2. One controller keyed on predicted admission time. It spans turns that have not yet arrived and turns already queued, and sets three things: the SSD fetch start (EDF, with a lead that accounts for the read backlog), the L2 protection horizon and budget, and the eviction order.
   - Relative to CachedAttention, this turns a window counted in jobs into a time horizon that also covers agent sessions still in their tool gap.
   - Relative to TokenCake and Ask the Tool, it extends the lead time to a contended SSD tier where fetches take seconds, and adds a queue-wait term.
   - None of the sources examined combines these.
3. A robustness study. Gap misprediction has an asymmetric cost: over-estimates only lose the gain, while under-estimates cost parking space and SSD re-reads. The fallback guarantees no regime does worse than today.

Honest framing: "forestall for agentic KV tiers", an incremental systems contribution. Its strength depends on two results:
- beating upstream's reactive re-query in the dense regime by a clear margin;
- keeping most of the oracle gain in the sparse regime with realistic, non-oracle gap prediction.

Two threats could shrink it:
- If the reactive admission re-query alone removes most dense-regime recompute, the remaining contribution is sparse-regime SSD timing. That is closest to TokenCake and Ask the Tool, and weaker.
- If reclaiming the mirror alone cuts x70 SSD returns from about 21% to 3-5%, as the LRU model predicts, the sparse-regime case also shrinks.
open_questions: Does a reactive admission-time L3 re-query alone break the x10/x1 recompute loop? Candidates are the upstream #40042 port and the local paced retry with tuned intervals. If it removes most of the recompute, the proactive part of Takeaway 2 saves only about 1 s of read time plus backlog per admission, which is small against a queue of about 100 s.

How predictable are real tool-return times, by tool type, in SWE-agent runs? These replays use deterministic trace gaps × scale. Session-history predictors fail on exactly the turns that end up on L3, because those have long gaps. Is a harness hint or live progress signal required?

How does the closed loop shift once recompute stops? Admission rate, queue depth and SSD read demand (37% of the SSD at today's rate) will all change. Device KV (668K tokens, about 24 contexts of 28K) may keep x1 queued even without recompute. At the same x70 load, the no-SSD arm averaged 59.5 s TTFT versus 1.5-1.9 s for the SSD arms, which suggests the regime depends partly on the cache policy.
Is the dense collapse bistable (metastable), or purely driven by capacity? The live set exceeds L1+L2 for 42-48% of the x10/x1 runs, so some L3 traffic is unavoidable even with perfect ordering.

Should protected content get soft eviction priority or a hard host lock? A hard lock can make write-through backups skip when evict_host cannot free enough space (unified_radix_cache.py:1412-1414). This has not happened so far (0 occurrences).

Does the nixl backend deduplicate h2s writes of recomputed pages, whose page hashes are identical? If not, about 0.6 GiB/s at x1 (57.97M tokens × 98,304 B over roughly 8,600 s) is spent rewriting pages L3 already holds.

How do the capacity lever and the timing lever combine at x70? The capacity lever reclaims the ~40% L2 mirror and demotes device evictions straight to L3. The LRU model predicts that reclaiming alone cuts SSD/cold returns from 21% to 2.7-4.5%.

Upstream semantics differ from this fork. Upstream (and HiRadixCache) keeps staged L3 pages pinned outside the tree until finalisation (#32724) and adds the admission re-query. The diagnosis, including the literal case where prefetched pages are evicted before use, must be re-checked after rebasing.
Would cache-aware admission remove the need for protection? This means admitting L2-resident requests first, as LPM or Strata-style deferral do. What would it cost in fairness and starvation?

Where does the regime switch lie between x70 and x10? There are no runs at x20-x50. How does the controller behave in the transition, where both early and late fetch are plausible and SSD reads compete with write-through?
With several instances, data parallelism, a shared L3 and a router, which instance serves the next turn (session affinity) changes the predicted admission time. How should the design handle that?
evaluation_plan: Step 0: fix the measurement before comparing anything. Pass aiohttp.TCPConnector(limit=0), or a limit of at least the session count, at replay_agentic.py:265 so that server arrival equals client send. Enable ReqTimeStats in every arm. Log per request: entry, admission, L3 enqueue/start/end, staged bytes, and protection start/end. Tag evict_host with the owning session where possible. Re-run baseline B0 at x70, x10 and x1, with at least 2-3 repetitions per arm (all current results are single runs).

Step 1: cheap falsification runs at x10/x1, which decide whether proactive timing is needed in the dense regime. (a) The local paced retry with interval ∈ {50, 500, 5,000} scheduling passes and a higher attempt cap. (b) Upstream's admission-time re-query, ported from #39283/#40042. (c) Queue-position eviction only (protect the queue head, evict the tail), with no fetch changes. Read out: recompute share, shared-prompt-only admission rate, host eviction rate, TTFT and admissions/s.

Step 2: oracle headroom. Give the design an oracle predicted admission time: the replay's known next arrival (end of reply + gap_slept) plus FCFS position with the measured admission rate. This bounds the benefit per regime. Proposed gate: if B3 (the reactive re-query) brings recompute below about 10% and is within about 10% of the oracle TTFT at x10/x1, drop proactive timing from the dense-regime claim.

Step 3: realistic prediction. Try four predictors: per-tool-type quantiles learned online (tool name taken from the generated tool call in the SWE-bench traces), session history, a harness-declared duration, and a progress-signal variant if the harness can emit one. Also re-run with stochastic gaps resampled from per-tool distributions, so the replay is not deterministic.

Workloads and regimes: gap scale x70, x40, x20, x10, x5 and x1 (to map where the regime switches); 64, 128 and 192 sessions; L2 of 80, 160 and 240 GB; SSD bandwidth at 1x and throttled to 0.5x; prefetch_threshold 256 vs 64.

Baselines: B0 arrival-time prefetch (three_tier_to, three_tier_wc). B1 hbm_host and hbm_lru. B2 local paced retry. B3 upstream reactive re-query. B4 CachedAttention look-ahead (prefetch window of Cmem/Skv jobs plus eviction exemption). B5 PCR (fixed 4-request window plus look-ahead LRU). B6 TokenCake / Ask-the-Tool style: refresh one transfer time before the predicted return, with no queue or backlog term and no protection. B7 write_back (non-inclusive L1/L2). B8 LPM cache-aware admission. B9 (optional) Cake-style compute-while-loading.

Metrics: returning-turn TTFT (mean, p50, p90, p99) by tier (device, host, SSD, recompute) and by regime; server wait (entry to admission) and client lag, reported separately; tokens recomputed after arrival and their share of prefill; shared-prompt-only admission rate; admissions/s and per-session makespan; SSD read and write GiB, utilization and read amplification (bytes read / bytes used); deadline misses (fetch finished after admission); staged and protected bytes and waste (evicted or unused before admission); host eviction rate; backup skips; GPU prefill time share.

Ablations: timing terms (read size only, + L3 backlog, + queue wait); EDF vs FIFO reads; protection off, soft priority or hard lock; horizon H ∈ {5, 10, 20, 30, 60 s} and budget β; eviction key LRU vs predicted admission; admission re-check on/off; quantile q ∈ {0.1, 0.25, 0.5}; mirror reclaim with L3-only demotion on/off.

Robustness: inject gap-prediction error e ∈ {−50, −25, 0, +25, +50}% plus heavy-tailed noise. Check that the worst case never falls below B0 (the fallback holds), and report SSD read amplification and staging waste.

Proposed success criteria. At x70: storage-hit TTFT p50 at or below about 0.5 s, and mean returning TTFT within about 15% of the oracle with realistic predictors. At x10/x1: recompute share below 10%, with better TTFT and admissions/s than B3. In every regime: no worse than B0, and SSD read amplification at or below about 1.2x.
headroom_estimates: x70 sparse regime, Takeaway 1 upper bound (oracle arrival, EDF, 20 s lead). Storage-hit TTFT mean 5.18 → 1.27 s (three_tier_to) and 5.57 → 0.32 s (three_tier_wc). A contention-free counterfactual gives 1.11 / 0.23 s. Mean returning TTFT 1.94 → 1.17 s (−40%) and 1.48 → 0.50 s (−66%). Addressable set: 19.7% / 18.6% of returning turns.

x70 with realistic leads. A 10 s lead hides 81-91% of fetch time (storage-hit TTFT mean 1.63 / 1.32 s). A lead of only the own read time hides 16-24%. Without protection, fetched content is re-evicted at 1% / 5-7% / 20-25% / 56-64% for leads of 10 / 20 / 30 / 60 s, and at 77% when fetching at the end of the reply. At 10-20 s leads, parked content averages 5-14% of L2 (peak 27%).

x70 limited by prediction. With a 2 s margin, a −25% gap error still nets 85-88% and −50% nets 55-63%. An over-estimate of 25% or more nets about 0-1%: it falls back to today's behaviour. Session-history predictors net 54-71% and add 500-700 GiB of extra SSD reads (against 1,571-1,810 GiB actually read).

x70 competing capacity lever. Reclaiming the roughly 40% of L2 that mirrors L1 (about 651K tokens, about 64 GB) would raise unique capacity from 1.64-1.66M to 2.30M tokens. A session-level LRU model predicts SSD/cold returns fall from 21.0% to 2.7-4.5%, which would shrink Takeaway 1's addressable set 4-8x. This is a model estimate, not a measurement.

x10/x1 dense regime, Takeaway 2 upper bound on work. 49.4-54.4M recomputed tokens are 93-95% of all prefill. 98.4-99.6% of these turns had their context in L1+L2 at arrival, and all of it was on SSD. At x1, new prefill per admitted turn would fall from about 20.7K tokens (7,490 tok/s ÷ 0.362 admissions/s) to about 1.0-1.1K. Write-through and SSD writes would fall from 54-58M tokens to roughly the x70 level of about 5M, so host eviction pressure (about 7K tok/s) would drop about 10x.

x10/x1 bandwidth. Reloading every admitted context just in time at x1 needs about 0.6-0.7 GiB/s, i.e. 32-37% of the 1.88 GiB/s SSD. Per-read throughput is 1.85-3.12 GiB/s at p50. Queue-aware eviction reduces this to the part of the queue that does not fit in L2 (queued private context 0.9-1.8M tokens vs at most 0.96M of host-only L2). Today's SSD write stream at x1 is about 0.6 GiB/s, mostly rewriting recomputed pages.

x10/x1 protection cost. A 10 s protection horizon at x1 holds about 0.362/s × 10 s × 20.6K ≈ 75K tokens, about 5% of L2. Pinning the whole queue would need about 1.59M tokens, roughly all of L2, which is infeasible.

x10/x1 TTFT cannot be estimated from these runs. The load is closed-loop, so recompute is both a symptom and a cause of the 100-110 s mean queue. At the same x70 load, hbm_host averaged 59.5 s TTFT against 1.5-1.9 s for the SSD arms, so recovering lost contexts can shift the operating point by an order of magnitude. x10/x1 still has to be measured. About 15% of x1 TTFT (19.9 s of 131.2 s) is client-side connection-cap lag, which no server change can remove.

The literal Takeaway 2 case, where prefetched L3 pages are evicted before admission, is small on its own. It wasted 0.91-0.94M (x10) and 0.21M (x1) SSD tokens that were read and discarded, 80-87% of real L3 reads. That is only 0.4-1.9% of lost tokens.

Inclusion at x10/x1. The total mirror is still about 39% of L2, but only 3-6.7% of L2 is idle mirror. The live set is at or above L1+L2 for 42-48% of the run. Reclaiming the mirror therefore helps much less in the dense regime than at x70.
